TITLE: Likelihood-shift scores for context use and memory use in retrieval-augmented answers
PROPOSAL: We define two scores that need no choice of attention heads or layers. The context score is the gain in log-likelihood of the generated answer when the retrieved documents are present compared with when they are replaced by unrelated documents of matched length. The memory score is the log-likelihood of the same answer under a closed-book prompt relative to the likelihood of a model-free reference answer. TITLE: Behavioral reliance scores from counterfactual document edits
PROPOSAL: We measure context use behaviorally rather than through internal activations. For each query we create edited copies of the retrieved documents in which one fact that the answer depends on is replaced by a plausible alternative, using a span-replacement model. The context score of an answer is the probability, estimated under the generator with sampling, that the answer follows the edited fact when the edit is present. The memory score is the probability that the generator reproduces its original claim under a closed-book prompt. An answer whose memory score exceeds its context score is flagged. The procedure needs only sampling access and runs on API models too. We test on RAGTruth and on a fresh news question set with answers dated after the training cutoff of Llama-3-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct.
CONTROLS: ReDeEP and the semantic entropy probe as white-box references on the open models, SelfCheckGPT and a prompted judge as black-box references, a placebo edit that changes a fact the answer does not depend on, and an ablation that scores with a scorer model different from the generator, with bootstrap confidence intervals over queries.
COST: 240
PREDICTION: Behavioral scores should reach AUROC within a few points of ReDeEP on RAGTruth and transfer to the news set without any refitting, where ReDeEP degrades. If edits are too easy to detect as out of place, the generator may ignore them regardless of grounding, which would flatten the context score and break the detector.

TITLE: Validating utilization scores on documents with planted facts
PROPOSAL: Existing scores are checked only by correlation with hallucination labels, never by whether they track use of the documents. We build a validation suite in which reliance is known by construction. In the first part, the documents contain facts invented for the study, so no model can know them, and a correct answer must come from the documents. In the second part, the documents contradict well-known facts, so a correct answer under the documents reveals context use while the familiar answer reveals memory use. In the third part, the documents are irrelevant and the answer can only come from memory. We score answers from two open-weights instruction-tuned models of seven and seventy billion parameters with likelihood-shift scores that require no layer or head choice, and we ask whether the scores separate the three parts and predict which source each answer followed. We then test the same scores as a hallucination detector on RAGTruth.
CONTROLS: Reimplemented ReDeEP scores on the same suite, raw perplexity and answer length as floors, a prompted judge asked which source the answer used, human annotation of source on a sample of answers, a placebo where documents are shuffled across queries, and bootstrap intervals over queries.
COST: 120
PREDICTION: Likelihood-shift scores should classify the source of an answer with accuracy well above the perplexity floor and above the reimplemented ReDeEP scores on the invented-fact part. They may fail on the contradiction part if the models refuse or hedge, producing answers that follow neither source.

TITLE: Claim-level grounding and recall scores as a black-box utilization detector
PROPOSAL: We decompose each generated answer into atomic claims with a claim splitter, then score every claim twice. The context score of a claim is the entailment probability given the retrieved documents from an off-the-shelf verifier such as MiniCheck. The memory score of a claim is the probability that the generator asserts the same claim when asked the question without documents, estimated from ten closed-book samples with a claim matcher. An answer is scored by the largest gap between memory score and context score over its claims, so no attention head, layer or model internals enter the computation, and the generator may be any model with sampling access. We run the detector on RAGTruth with Llama-3-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and on a data-to-text split where tables are the documents.
CONTROLS: ReDeEP and the semantic entropy probe on the open models, the verifier alone without the memory score, the memory score alone, SelfCheckGPT, a prompted judge, a placebo that matches closed-book samples to claims from a different answer, and three seeds for the sampled closed-book answers.
COST: 160
PREDICTION: The gap score should beat the verifier alone by several AUROC points on question answering, because unsupported claims that the model also states closed-book are the typical hallucination. The detector could fail on data-to-text, where closed-book sampling yields nothing comparable and the memory score collapses to zero for every claim.

Problem statement:
Time-series forecasting is a fundamental task in machine learning, aiming to predict future events based on past observations. It is of practical importance, as it plays a crucial role in many real-world applications, including weather forecasting, electricity consumption forecasting, and traffic flow prediction. Despite decades of rapid advances in machine learning, time-series forecasting remains a challenging problem due to complex temporal dependencies, non-linear patterns, domain variability, and other factors. In recent years, numerous deep learning approaches have been proposed to improve forecasting accuracy, and it continues to be an active area of research.

In multivariate time-series forecasting, each time step carries an observation of C variables (or channels), and the goal is to predict the future values of all variables over a forecasting horizon of length H, given a lookback window of the L most recent observations. Solving the task requires effectively capturing key characteristics of time-series data, such as temporal dependencies and cross-variable interactions. A common approach is to design a forecasting architecture that can model such properties and to train it with a simple objective, such as the mean squared error between the predicted and ground-truth future values.

One promising and popular research direction is to design new neural network architectures for time-series data, such as Transformers, convolutional neural networks, multi-layer perceptrons, and state space models. These architectures primarily focus on capturing temporal and channel (i.e., variate) dependencies within input signals, that is, on how to encode the input into a meaningful representation. Encoder architectures are often categorized into two groups: channel-independent encoders, which treat each variate separately and apply the same encoder across all variates, and channel-dependent encoders, which explicitly model interactions among variates. Channel-independent encoders are considered simple yet robust; however, they fundamentally overlook cross-channel interactions, which can be critical for multivariate time-series forecasting. In contrast, channel-dependent encoders can inherently capture such cross-channel dependencies, but they often suffer from high computational cost and do not consistently yield significant improvements in forecasting accuracy over channel-independent baselines.

While the encoder architecture is undoubtedly a core component of time-series forecasting models, it is equally important to consider (i) how to accurately predict (i.e., decode) future signals from the encoded representations of past signals, and (ii) how to effectively train the entire forecasting model. However, these aspects have often been studied independently, and little attention has been paid to how to effectively integrate them. For decoding, most prior works rely on a simple linear projection that directly predicts the future from the encoded representations. This design offers advantages in terms of simplicity and training efficiency, but may struggle to fully capture complex temporal structures. For training, inspired by BERT, masking-and-reconstruction tasks have been commonly adopted to pretrain encoders before supervised learning for time-series forecasting: a subset of temporal segments is masked, and the encoder learns to reconstruct the masked portions. Despite its effectiveness, it remains questionable whether this self-supervised objective and the two-stage (pretraining-finetuning) training strategy are truly aligned with the architectural designs (i.e., encoders and decoders) of time-series forecasting models.

This leaves several open questions. How should the encoding of inputs, the decoding of predictions, and the training of a multivariate forecasting model be considered jointly rather than in isolation? Can cross-channel dependencies be exploited without the high computational cost and inconsistent accuracy gains of existing channel-dependent encoders? Is there a better way than a simple linear projection to produce predictions from encoded representations? And can the training objective be aligned with the model's architecture so that the model learns temporal dynamics more effectively, without depending on a separate pretraining-finetuning pipeline?

TITLE: One model, one objective: encoder, cross-channel mixing and query decoder trained together
PROPOSAL: We build a forecaster whose three parts are designed for each other. The encoder is a channel-independent patch transformer; after it, a low-rank mixing layer lets each variate attend to a small set of learned channel prototypes rather than to all other variates, which keeps the cross-channel step linear in the number of channels. PREDICTION: The joint model should beat PatchTST on Electricity and Traffic, where cross-channel structure matters, and match it on the ETT sets, with throughput close to PatchTST. The gain could vanish if the prototype mixing collapses onto a single prototype, which the ablation would reveal.

TITLE: Masked-future prediction as a single-stage objective aligned with the forecaster

TITLE: Coarse-to-fine decoding of the forecast horizon
PROPOSAL: We decode the future at several temporal resolutions. The encoder, a channel-independent patch transformer, produces representations of the past. Problem statement:
Time-series forecasting is a fundamental task in machine learning, aiming to predict future events based on past observations. It is of practical importance, as it plays a crucial role in many real-world applications, including weather forecasting, electricity consumption forecasting, and traffic flow prediction. Despite decades of rapid advances in machine learning, time-series forecasting remains a challenging problem due to complex temporal dependencies, non-linear patterns, domain variability, and other factors. In recent years, numerous deep learning approaches have been proposed to improve forecasting accuracy, and it continues to be an active area of research.

In multivariate time-series forecasting, each time step carries an observation of C variables (or channels), and the goal is to predict the future values of all variables over a forecasting horizon of length H, given a lookback window of the L most recent observations. Solving the task requires effectively capturing key characteristics of time-series data, such as temporal dependencies and cross-variable interactions. A common approach is to design a forecasting architecture that can model such properties and to train it with a simple objective, such as the mean squared error between the predicted and ground-truth future values.

One promising and popular research direction is to design new neural network architectures for time-series data, such as Transformers, convolutional neural networks, multi-layer perceptrons, and state space models. These architectures primarily focus on capturing temporal and channel (i.e., variate) dependencies within input signals, that is, on how to encode the input into a meaningful representation. Encoder architectures are often categorized into two groups: channel-independent encoders, which treat each variate separately and apply the same encoder across all variates, and channel-dependent encoders, which explicitly model interactions among variates. Channel-independent encoders are considered simple yet robust; however, they fundamentally overlook cross-channel interactions, which can be critical for multivariate time-series forecasting. In contrast, channel-dependent encoders can inherently capture such cross-channel dependencies, but they often suffer from high computational cost and do not consistently yield significant improvements in forecasting accuracy over channel-independent baselines.

While the encoder architecture is undoubtedly a core component of time-series forecasting models, it is equally important to consider (i) how to accurately predict (i.e., decode) future signals from the encoded representations of past signals, and (ii) how to effectively train the entire forecasting model. However, these aspects have often been studied independently, and little attention has been paid to how to effectively integrate them. For decoding, most prior works rely on a simple linear projection that directly predicts the future from the encoded representations. This design offers advantages in terms of simplicity and training efficiency, but may struggle to fully capture complex temporal structures. For training, inspired by BERT, masking-and-reconstruction tasks have been commonly adopted to pretrain encoders before supervised learning for time-series forecasting: a subset of temporal segments is masked, and the encoder learns to reconstruct the masked portions. Despite its effectiveness, it remains questionable whether this self-supervised objective and the two-stage (pretraining-finetuning) training strategy are truly aligned with the architectural designs (i.e., encoders and decoders) of time-series forecasting models.

This leaves several open questions. How should the encoding of inputs, the decoding of predictions, and the training of a multivariate forecasting model be considered jointly rather than in isolation? Can cross-channel dependencies be exploited without the high computational cost and inconsistent accuracy gains of existing channel-dependent encoders? Is there a better way than a simple linear projection to produce predictions from encoded representations? And can the training objective be aligned with the model's architecture so that the model learns temporal dynamics more effectively, without depending on a separate pretraining-finetuning pipeline?

Problem statement:
Self-supervised contrastive learning has become a cornerstone paradigm for representation learning, enabling models to extract rich semantic features without explicit labels. At its core, contrastive learning constructs a latent space in which semantically similar samples (different augmented views of the same instance) converge while dissimilar samples diverge, and it is frequently guided by information-theoretic objectives such as maximizing the mutual information between views. Its empirical success has motivated extensive theoretical work: contrastive objectives have been decomposed into alignment and uniformity principles, related to mutual information maximization and noise contrastive estimation, and connected to spectral clustering on a data graph. Despite these advances, a fundamental tension persists between theoretical understanding and practical implementation. Existing analyses offer limited insight into the dynamic information landscape that unfolds during the learning process, in particular into how much new information the views presented to the model actually contribute for each individual instance.

In practice, current contrastive frameworks such as SimCLR, MoCo and their variants rely heavily on static, human-engineered augmentations and on large-batch sampling to enforce invariance and representational diversity. These choices impose rigid constraints on the learning dynamics: augmentations must balance semantic preservation against transformational complexity, while batch scaling faces unavoidable hardware limitations. Despite substantial engineering efforts to refine augmentation strategies, these methods fundamentally lack a principled mechanism for adaptively expanding the representational capacity of each instance while maintaining semantic coherence.

This leaves several open questions. How can the information gained through the views of an instance be characterized in a principled, information-theoretic way, so that augmentation design is guided by more than heuristics? Can the diversity of views be expanded adaptively and in a controlled manner, rather than only through fixed hand-crafted augmentation pipelines or ever larger batches, without sacrificing the semantic consistency that views of the same instance must share? And how should the trade-off between semantic invariance and representational expressivity be managed so that contrastive learning remains effective in small-batch, hardware-constrained settings?

TITLE: Per-instance view information gain estimated with a conditional entropy bound
PROPOSAL: We quantify, for each training image, how much a given augmented view adds beyond what the model already encodes, using a conditional entropy estimate computed from the embedding of the anchor and of the view under a small variational decoder trained alongside a SimCLR encoder. We train a ResNet-18 on CIFAR-100 and ImageNet-100 with the standard augmentation set, log the per-instance gain for each augmentation family across training, and relate it to the final linear probe accuracy of the classes those instances belong to. TITLE: Feature-space view expansion gated by neighbourhood agreement at small batch
PROPOSAL: We generate additional positive views for each instance directly in the embedding space of a MoCo v2 encoder by moving the anchor embedding along directions sampled from the covariance of its nearest neighbours in the queue, and we admit a synthetic view only when its nearest-neighbour label agreement with the anchor, measured on a frozen copy of the encoder, stays above a threshold set on a validation split. Training runs on STL-10 and ImageNet-100 with a ResNet-50 at batch sizes of 64 and 256, and we evaluate linear probe and kNN accuracy as well as alignment and uniformity on the test set.
CONTROLS: The comparison includes the same encoder trained with image-space augmentations only at both batch sizes, the same encoder at batch 1024 as an upper reference point, synthetic views drawn along random isotropic directions of the same norm, and synthetic views admitted without the agreement gate, so that the contribution of the gate can be separated from that of the expansion itself.
COST: 420
PREDICTION: Gated expansion should close most of the gap between batch 64 and batch 1024 on ImageNet-100 kNN accuracy, while ungated expansion should degrade alignment. If random directions perform as well as covariance directions, the neighbourhood structure is not what helps.

Problem statement:
Self-supervised contrastive learning has become a cornerstone paradigm for representation learning, enabling models to extract rich semantic features without explicit labels. At its core, contrastive learning constructs a latent space in which semantically similar samples (different augmented views of the same instance) converge while dissimilar samples diverge, and it is frequently guided by information-theoretic objectives such as maximizing the mutual information between views. Its empirical success has motivated extensive theoretical work: contrastive objectives have been decomposed into alignment and uniformity principles, related to mutual information maximization and noise contrastive estimation, and connected to spectral clustering on a data graph. Despite these advances, a fundamental tension persists between theoretical understanding and practical implementation. Existing analyses offer limited insight into the dynamic information landscape that unfolds during the learning process, in particular into how much new information the views presented to the model actually contribute for each individual instance.

In practice, current contrastive frameworks such as SimCLR, MoCo and their variants rely heavily on static, human-engineered augmentations and on large-batch sampling to enforce invariance and representational diversity. These choices impose rigid constraints on the learning dynamics: augmentations must balance semantic preservation against transformational complexity, while batch scaling faces unavoidable hardware limitations. Despite substantial engineering efforts to refine augmentation strategies, these methods fundamentally lack a principled mechanism for adaptively expanding the representational capacity of each instance while maintaining semantic coherence.

This leaves several open questions. How can the information gained through the views of an instance be characterized in a principled, information-theoretic way, so that augmentation design is guided by more than heuristics? Can the diversity of views be expanded adaptively and in a controlled manner, rather than only through fixed hand-crafted augmentation pipelines or ever larger batches, without sacrificing the semantic consistency that views of the same instance must share? And how should the trade-off between semantic invariance and representational expressivity be managed so that contrastive learning remains effective in small-batch, hardware-constrained settings?

TITLE: Small-batch contrastive learning with per-instance adaptive temperature driven by view agreement
PROPOSAL: We test whether the trade-off between invariance and expressivity can be managed per instance by setting the InfoNCE temperature of each anchor from the agreement between its views: anchors whose views already agree closely receive a lower temperature that sharpens separation from neighbours, while anchors whose views disagree receive a higher temperature that tolerates the spread. Agreement is the cosine similarity between view embeddings under a momentum encoder. We train ResNet-18 and ResNet-50 encoders on CIFAR-100, Tiny-ImageNet and ImageNet-100 at batch sizes 32, 128 and 512 and measure linear probe accuracy, kNN accuracy, alignment and uniformity.
CONTROLS: A fixed temperature tuned per batch size, a global temperature schedule that decays over training, a temperature assigned from a shuffled agreement vector, and the same adaptive rule applied to a MoCo variant with a queue so that the effect is not specific to in-batch negatives, each over three seeds.
COST: 480
PREDICTION: Adaptive temperature should help most at batch 32, narrowing the gap to batch 512 by roughly a third on ImageNet-100, and should give nothing at batch 512. If the shuffled assignment performs the same, the gain comes from the temperature distribution rather than from instance-level matching.

TITLE: A controlled synthetic benchmark for separating semantic invariance from view expressivity
PROPOSAL: We construct an image dataset from a rendering pipeline in which each instance has known semantic factors (object identity and shape) and known nuisance factors (pose, lighting, background and texture), so that for any augmentation the information shared between views and the information lost about each factor can be computed exactly from the generative model. COST: 150
PREDICTION: Linear probe accuracy on identity should rise and pose accuracy fall monotonically as the augmentation randomises more nuisance factors, with the crossing point predicted by the computed information quantities. The prediction fails if the exact quantities and the measured probe accuracies disagree on which augmentation setting is best, which would indicate that optimisation effects dominate the information picture.

TITLE: Replacing large batches with an instance-conditioned negative bank for hardware-constrained contrastive training
PROPOSAL: We ask whether the diversity usually obtained from large batches can be recovered by maintaining, for each instance, a small set of hard negatives selected by a momentum encoder from a queue and refreshed every epoch, so that each anchor sees a few informative negatives instead of thousands of random ones. PREDICTION: Selected negatives should recover most of the kNN accuracy of the large-batch reference at batch 64, but the false negative rate should rise as selection becomes harder. We expect the random bank to perform no better than the standard queue.

TITLE: Replacing large batches with an instance-conditioned negative bank for hardware-constrained contrastive training
PROPOSAL: We ask whether the diversity usually obtained from large batches can be recovered by maintaining, for each instance, a small set of hard negatives selected by a momentum encoder from a queue and refreshed every epoch, so that each anchor sees a few informative negatives instead of thousands of random ones. TITLE: Does the augmentation graph spectrum tell us when more views stop helping
PROPOSAL: We examine the claim that contrastive learning performs spectral clustering on an augmentation graph by measuring, on real datasets, how the spectrum of the empirical augmentation kernel changes as augmentation strength increases, and whether the eigenvalue decay predicts the information that further views add. TITLE: Diffusion-generated views under a per-instance semantic distance target for small-batch SimCLR
PROPOSAL: We expand the set of views per instance with samples from a class-agnostic image diffusion model conditioned on the anchor through an image-to-image process with noise strength chosen per instance. The noise strength is raised until the cosine similarity between anchor and generated view under a frozen pretrained encoder drops to a target level, so that every instance receives views of comparable semantic distance rather than comparable pixel distortion. We train SimCLR with a ResNet-50 on ImageNet-100 at batch sizes 64 and 256, mixing one generated view with one standard view per instance, and evaluate linear probe and kNN accuracy, alignment and uniformity, and transfer to CIFAR-100.
CONTROLS: Standard augmentations alone at both batch sizes and at batch 2048, generated views at a fixed noise strength for all instances, generated views from an unconditioned diffusion sample matched to the anchor only by class, and views produced by strong hand-crafted augmentation tuned to the same average similarity, three seeds each.
COST: 1100
PREDICTION: Per-instance noise strength should outperform fixed strength and should narrow the gap between batch 64 and batch 2048 by about half. Class-matched unconditioned samples should hurt alignment, confirming that the gain needs instance-level conditioning.

TITLE: View scheduling from running per-instance information estimates
PROPOSAL: We allocate the number of augmented views drawn per instance in each epoch according to a running estimate of how much its recent views disagreed in embedding space, giving more views to instances whose views still carry fresh information and fewer to instances whose views have converged. Problem statement:
Vision-language models (VLMs) such as CLIP learn to align visual and textual representations in a shared embedding space, enabling effective performance on a wide range of multi-modal tasks such as image classification, multi-modal retrieval and semantic segmentation. The introduction of natural language gives VLMs better flexibility and generalization than traditional visual classification models. To further enhance their performance, numerous training-time approaches, such as prompt learning from labeled data, have been proposed, introducing effective optimization solutions and inference paradigms.

In contrast to training-time approaches, test-time adaptation (TTA) methods have attracted increasing attention for their ability to enhance the performance of VLMs during inference without requiring additional annotated data. Depending on the type of test data, TTA methods can be broadly categorized into episodic and online strategies. Episodic TTA adapts the model to a single test sample, exploring the information inside that sample to improve the model's prediction. Online TTA processes a stream of test data, using historical knowledge from previously seen samples to update model behavior. A growing number of methods of both kinds have been proposed, each typically reporting gains over earlier ones.

However, existing TTA research for VLMs suffers from various limitations in experimental setup and analysis. First, most works rely on reported baseline results without reproducing them under consistent experimental settings. This leads to unfair comparisons due to variations in pre-trained model checkpoints, text prompts and evaluation protocols, so it is unclear how much of the reported progress reflects genuine algorithmic improvement. Second, except for a few works that explore alternative evaluation metrics, the majority of research focuses narrowly on accuracy, resulting in an incomplete understanding of what adaptation does to a model, even though real-world deployment requires models that are also reliable and robust. Third, there is a lack of systematic evaluation of TTA methods on models that have already been tuned at training time and on VLM architectures beyond CLIP, which limits the generalizability of existing conclusions. Together, these problems hinder fair comparisons between TTA methods and make it difficult to assess their practical strengths and weaknesses.

This raises several open questions. When existing episodic and online TTA methods are compared under consistent and controlled conditions, how much do they actually improve over the unadapted model, and how much real progress have recent methods made over the earliest ones? Do their gains generalize to VLMs other than CLIP, and does test-time adaptation complement or conflict with training-time fine-tuning of the model? Finally, beyond classification accuracy, does accuracy-oriented test-time adaptation preserve or compromise the trustworthiness and stability that practitioners need for reliable deployment?

Problem statement:
Vision-language models (VLMs) such as CLIP learn to align visual and textual representations in a shared embedding space, enabling effective performance on a wide range of multi-modal tasks such as image classification, multi-modal retrieval and semantic segmentation. The introduction of natural language gives VLMs better flexibility and generalization than traditional visual classification models. To further enhance their performance, numerous training-time approaches, such as prompt learning from labeled data, have been proposed, introducing effective optimization solutions and inference paradigms.

In contrast to training-time approaches, test-time adaptation (TTA) methods have attracted increasing attention for their ability to enhance the performance of VLMs during inference without requiring additional annotated data. Depending on the type of test data, TTA methods can be broadly categorized into episodic and online strategies. Episodic TTA adapts the model to a single test sample, exploring the information inside that sample to improve the model's prediction. Online TTA processes a stream of test data, using historical knowledge from previously seen samples to update model behavior. A growing number of methods of both kinds have been proposed, each typically reporting gains over earlier ones.

However, existing TTA research for VLMs suffers from various limitations in experimental setup and analysis. First, most works rely on reported baseline results without reproducing them under consistent experimental settings. This leads to unfair comparisons due to variations in pre-trained model checkpoints, text prompts and evaluation protocols, so it is unclear how much of the reported progress reflects genuine algorithmic improvement. Second, except for a few works that explore alternative evaluation metrics, the majority of research focuses narrowly on accuracy, resulting in an incomplete understanding of what adaptation does to a model, even though real-world deployment requires models that are also reliable and robust. Third, there is a lack of systematic evaluation of TTA methods on models that have already been tuned at training time and on VLM architectures beyond CLIP, which limits the generalizability of existing conclusions. Together, these problems hinder fair comparisons between TTA methods and make it difficult to assess their practical strengths and weaknesses.

When existing episodic and online TTA methods are compared under consistent and controlled conditions, how much do they actually improve over the unadapted model, and how much real progress have recent methods made over the earliest ones? Do their gains generalize to VLMs other than CLIP, and does test-time adaptation complement or conflict with training-time fine-tuning of the model? TITLE: Does test-time adaptation compound with prompt learning or cancel it
PROPOSAL: We take CLIP ViT-B/16 checkpoints already tuned at training time with CoOp, CoCoOp, MaPLe and PromptSRC on the 16-shot ImageNet protocol, then apply two episodic methods, TPT and MTA, and two online methods, TDA and DPE, at test time on ImageNet, ImageNet-A, ImageNet-R, ImageNet-Sketch, ImageNet-V2 and the fine-grained transfer datasets. TITLE: What test-time adaptation does to calibration, selective prediction and shift detection
PROPOSAL: We measure, beyond accuracy, what adaptation does to the reliability of CLIP ViT-B/16 predictions: expected calibration error, negative log-likelihood, area under the risk-coverage curve for selective prediction, and the AUROC of maximum softmax probability for separating ImageNet from ImageNet-O as an out-of-distribution detection task. Methods are TPT, C-TPT, MTA, TDA and DPE, run on ImageNet, ImageNet-A, ImageNet-R and the fine-grained datasets. We report every metric before and after adaptation for the same test images, so that each method is characterised by a vector of changes rather than a single accuracy delta.
CONTROLS: The unadapted model, temperature scaling of the unadapted model fitted on a held-out split as a calibration-only baseline, each method with its confidence-selection step disabled, and three stream orders for the online methods.
COST: 48
PREDICTION: Entropy-minimising methods should lower calibration error on the shifted sets while raising it on in-domain ImageNet, and the risk-coverage area should improve less than accuracy does. If temperature scaling alone matches the calibration changes, the adaptation adds nothing to reliability beyond a confidence rescaling.

TITLE: Stability of online test-time adaptation under stream order and label shift
PROPOSAL: We test whether online methods for CLIP keep their accuracy when the test stream changes character: we run TDA, DMN, DPE and BoostAdapter on ImageNet-R, ImageNet-Sketch and the fine-grained datasets under four stream regimes, a random order, a class-sorted order, a stream with a sudden switch between two datasets, and a stream that repeats a small subset many times. We record accuracy over the stream in windows of 500 samples and calculate the variance of windowed accuracy and the worst window for each method. We also measure how fast each method recovers after the dataset switch.
CONTROLS: The unadapted model, each episodic method as an order-independent reference, each online method with its cache reset every window, and five random orders to bound the variance expected from sampling alone.
COST: 36
PREDICTION: Cache-based methods should lose several points under class-sorted streams and recover slowly after a switch, while episodic methods stay flat. If resetting the cache every window removes the loss, the instability sits in cache contents rather than in the update rule.

Vision-language models (VLMs) such as CLIP learn to align visual and textual representations in a shared embedding space, enabling effective performance on a wide range of multi-modal tasks such as image classification, multi-modal retrieval and semantic segmentation. The introduction of natural language gives VLMs better flexibility and generalization than traditional visual classification models. To further enhance their performance, numerous training-time approaches, such as prompt learning from labeled data, have been proposed, introducing effective optimization solutions and inference paradigms.

In contrast to training-time approaches, test-time adaptation (TTA) methods have attracted increasing attention for their ability to enhance the performance of VLMs during inference without requiring additional annotated data. Depending on the type of test data, TTA methods can be broadly categorized into episodic and online strategies. Episodic TTA adapts the model to a single test sample, exploring the information inside that sample to improve the model's prediction. Online TTA processes a stream of test data, using historical knowledge from previously seen samples to update model behavior. A growing number of methods of both kinds have been proposed, each typically reporting gains over earlier ones.

However, existing TTA research for VLMs suffers from various limitations in experimental setup and analysis. First, most works rely on reported baseline results without reproducing them under consistent experimental settings. This leads to unfair comparisons due to variations in pre-trained model checkpoints, text prompts and evaluation protocols, so it is unclear how much of the reported progress reflects genuine algorithmic improvement. Second, except for a few works that explore alternative evaluation metrics, the majority of research focuses narrowly on accuracy, resulting in an incomplete understanding of what adaptation does to a model, even though real-world deployment requires models that are also reliable and robust. Third, there is a lack of systematic evaluation of TTA methods on models that have already been tuned at training time and on VLM architectures beyond CLIP, which limits the generalizability of existing conclusions. Together, these problems hinder fair comparisons between TTA methods and make it difficult to assess their practical strengths and weaknesses.

This raises several open questions. When existing episodic and online TTA methods are compared under consistent and controlled conditions, how much do they actually improve over the unadapted model, and how much real progress have recent methods made over the earliest ones? Do their gains generalize to VLMs other than CLIP, and does test-time adaptation complement or conflict with training-time fine-tuning of the model? Finally, beyond classification accuracy, does accuracy-oriented test-time adaptation preserve or compromise the trustworthiness and stability that practitioners need for reliable deployment?

Problem statement:
Visual synthesis has witnessed remarkable progress in recent years, largely propelled by the scaling of Transformer architectures. Video generation in particular has attracted growing interest from both academia and industry, owing to its wide-ranging applications in content creation, world simulation and beyond. At present, diffusion models lead the field by iteratively denoising latent representations to produce high-fidelity clips. Concurrently, autoregressive models have been explored for their potential to unify image and video generation and to generalize over longer time horizons.

Despite their successes, each paradigm exhibits critical shortcomings. Video diffusion models excel at synthesizing fixed-length frame sequences by exploiting bidirectional attention, yet they incur substantial computational cost due to tens or even hundreds of sequential denoising steps, and they struggle to extend seamlessly to video extrapolation; their slow generation speed hinders the production of high-resolution, long-duration videos. Autoregressive methods based on next-token prediction, which predict video tokens in a fixed order (for example token by token along both spatial and temporal axes, as in Emu3, or set by set in space and then frame by frame in time, as in Nova), are inherently capable of streaming generation, but they often fall short in visual fidelity and require hundreds to tens of thousands of inference steps, resulting in prohibitive latency.

These observations motivate the need for a generation framework that simultaneously possesses high visual quality, efficiency and temporal generalization. In image synthesis, Visual AutoRegressive modeling (VAR) recently redefined generation as a coarse-to-fine next-scale prediction, and its follow-up, Infinity, introduced bitwise modeling and scaled up the vocabulary size, achieving performance comparable to diffusion models while offering significant advantages in inference speed. These advances, however, concern the spatial-only generation of static images. Whether a discrete autoregressive approach can deliver comparable quality and speed for video, where the temporal dimension, far larger token counts and the need for coherent motion come into play, remains an open question.

Several obstacles make this difficult. Discrete video tokenizers, on which purely discrete generators depend, are usually either trained from scratch, which is computationally heavy for clips of tens of frames and converges slowly, or initialized from discrete image tokenizers, whose weights are not optimal for video reconstruction. Long videos also imply long contexts: maintaining temporal consistency requires attending to previously generated content, yet attending to the full history leads to explosively long sequences and high computational cost.

The problem is therefore to design a single, purely discrete autoregressive model that generates high-resolution (e.g., 720p) videos with visual quality competitive with leading diffusion models at much lower inference latency, while unifying text-to-image, text-to-video, image-to-video and video extrapolation within one framework, and extending to long, multi-round video generation that follows successive user instructions. How should the temporal dimension be modeled so that a single model serves both images and videos and faithfully captures both appearance and motion? How can discrete video tokenizers with high reconstruction quality be obtained without prohibitive training cost? And how can the cost of long spatiotemporal contexts be contained without sacrificing temporal consistency or visual quality?

Problem statement:
Visual synthesis has witnessed remarkable progress in recent years, largely propelled by the scaling of Transformer architectures. Video generation in particular has attracted growing interest from both academia and industry, owing to its wide-ranging applications in content creation, world simulation and beyond. At present, diffusion models lead the field by iteratively denoising latent representations to produce high-fidelity clips. Concurrently, autoregressive models have been explored for their potential to unify image and video generation and to generalize over longer time horizons.

Despite their successes, each paradigm exhibits critical shortcomings. Video diffusion models excel at synthesizing fixed-length frame sequences by exploiting bidirectional attention, yet they incur substantial computational cost due to tens or even hundreds of sequential denoising steps, and they struggle to extend seamlessly to video extrapolation; their slow generation speed hinders the production of high-resolution, long-duration videos. Autoregressive methods based on next-token prediction, which predict video tokens in a fixed order (for example token by token along both spatial and temporal axes, as in Emu3, or set by set in space and then frame by frame in time, as in Nova), are inherently capable of streaming generation, but they often fall short in visual fidelity and require hundreds to tens of thousands of inference steps, resulting in prohibitive latency.

These observations motivate the need for a generation framework that simultaneously possesses high visual quality, efficiency and temporal generalization. In image synthesis, Visual AutoRegressive modeling (VAR) recently redefined generation as a coarse-to-fine next-scale prediction, and its follow-up, Infinity, introduced bitwise modeling and scaled up the vocabulary size, achieving performance comparable to diffusion models while offering significant advantages in inference speed. These advances, however, concern the spatial-only generation of static images. Whether a discrete autoregressive approach can deliver comparable quality and speed for video, where the temporal dimension, far larger token counts and the need for coherent motion come into play, remains an open question.

Several obstacles make this difficult. Discrete video tokenizers, on which purely discrete generators depend, are usually either trained from scratch, which is computationally heavy for clips of tens of frames and converges slowly, or initialized from discrete image tokenizers, whose weights are not optimal for video reconstruction. Long videos also imply long contexts: maintaining temporal consistency requires attending to previously generated content, yet attending to the full history leads to explosively long sequences and high computational cost.

The problem is therefore to design a single, purely discrete autoregressive model that generates high-resolution (e.g., 720p) videos with visual quality competitive with leading diffusion models at much lower inference latency, while unifying text-to-image, text-to-video, image-to-video and video extrapolation within one framework, and extending to long, multi-round video generation that follows successive user instructions. How should the temporal dimension be modeled so that a single model serves both images and videos and faithfully captures both appearance and motion? How can discrete video tokenizers with high reconstruction quality be obtained without prohibitive training cost? And how can the cost of long spatiotemporal contexts be contained without sacrificing temporal consistency or visual quality?

Paper type: Experimental only
Data type: Mostly real-world data
Experimental domains: text-to-video generation, text-to-image generation, image-to-video generation, video extrapolation, long interactive video generation

TITLE: Scale-then-frame next-scale prediction for unified image and video generation
PROPOSAL: We extend Infinity-style bitwise next-scale prediction to video by treating each frame as a sequence of scales, ordering tokens scale-major within a frame and frame-major across time, so that an image is a one-frame video and the same model handles text-to-image, text-to-video and image-to-video by changing only the conditioning prefix. We train a 2B-parameter transformer on a mix of image-text pairs and 5-second clips at 480p, then adapt it to 720p with a short second stage.
CONTROLS: Baselines: a diffusion transformer of matched size trained on the same clips, an Emu3-style token-by-token raster model, and a frame-major variant that predicts all scales of frame t only after completing frame t-1. Ablations: scale-major against frame-major ordering, bitwise against index prediction, and the image share of the data mix at two levels.
COST: 2400
PREDICTION: Scale-major ordering within a frame should reach VBench scores within a few points of the diffusion baseline at under a tenth of its latency and beat the raster model on FVD on UCF-101. If motion smoothness lags far behind the diffusion model, the within-frame scale ordering is breaking temporal coupling and the frame-major variant should then win.

TITLE: Obtaining a discrete video tokenizer by temporal expansion of an image tokenizer
PROPOSAL: We take the bitwise image tokenizer of Infinity, replace each 2D convolution by a causal 3D convolution whose central temporal slice carries the image weights and whose other slices start at zero, and fine-tune only the temporal slices and the quantizer on 17-frame clips at 256p before unfreezing everything briefly at 480p. The first frame is encoded exactly as an image would be, so images and videos share one codebook and one decoder.
CONTROLS: We compare against the same architecture trained from scratch on the same clips, against a tokenizer with the image weights copied into every temporal slice, and against the plain 2D tokenizer applied frame by frame. Reconstruction is measured by PSNR, LPIPS and rFVD on UCF-101 and on a held-out web-video set, both at equal training steps and at the step where each tokenizer stops improving.
COST: 320
PREDICTION: The expanded tokenizer should reach the rFVD of the from-scratch tokenizer in a small fraction of its training steps and keep image reconstruction unchanged. If the frame-by-frame 2D tokenizer matches it on rFVD, temporal compression is not what the generator needs from the tokenizer and the gain must come from the generator side.

TITLE: Coarse-scale history for long video generation with bounded context
PROPOSAL: We give the generator a context made of the last four frames at every scale plus only the two coarsest scales of all earlier frames, so that the attended sequence grows slowly while global layout and identity remain visible. Training randomises the cut-off so the model learns to work with any history length, and we optimise for the generation of two-minute videos at 480p in rounds of eight seconds, each conditioned on a new instruction.
CONTROLS: Full-history attention up to the length that fits, a pure sliding window of four frames without any coarse history, a window that keeps only the first frame as anchor, and a key-value cache compressed by token merging at equal memory. We measure subject consistency and background consistency on VBench-Long, drift of CLIP similarity to the first frame over time, and per-frame latency as the video lengthens, over three seeds.
COST: 900
PREDICTION: Coarse-scale history should hold subject consistency within a few points of full attention while keeping per-frame latency flat, and beat the plain sliding window by a wide gap on background consistency. Failure would show up as the model ignoring the coarse history, in which case the first-frame anchor would match it.

TITLE: Latency against quality at 720p for next-scale video prediction
PROPOSAL: We train a Visual AutoRegressive (VAR) style video generator with bitwise next-scale prediction, using a sixteen-frame latent clip at 720p and a schedule of ten scales per frame, and we measure the full trade-off between visual quality and wall-clock latency on a single accelerator. Quality is read from the Fréchet Video Distance (FVD) on Kinetics-600 and from the VBench benchmark suite, and latency is the time from prompt to decoded clip, including the tokeniser decoder.
CONTROLS: A Diffusion Transformer (DiT) baseline of matched parameter count at fifty, twenty and eight denoising steps, a next-token raster autoregressive model with key-value (KV) caching, and our model with fewer scales per frame. The Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) scale is tuned separately for each model on a held-out prompt set so that no method is compared at a setting chosen for another.
COST: 1500

TITLE: Multi-round instruction-following video extension in one discrete model
PROPOSAL: We train the unified next-scale generator with a conversational format in which each round appends a text instruction and a continuation of forty-eight frames conditioned on the whole previous video through compressed history. Training clips are cut into segments with per-segment captions produced by a captioning model, so that the generator sees instruction changes in the middle of a video. We evaluate five-round generations in which each instruction changes the camera motion or an object action.
CONTROLS: A single-round model asked to regenerate the whole video with the concatenated instructions, a diffusion extension baseline that continues from the last frames only, and our model with the history truncated to the current round. Metrics: per-round instruction adherence judged by a vision-language model and checked by two raters, subject consistency across rounds, and the share of rounds in which motion follows the new instruction.
COST: 1100
PREDICTION: Round-by-round generation should follow new instructions in most rounds while keeping subject identity across rounds, and the diffusion extension baseline should drift on identity after the third round. The likely failure is that the generator ignores late instructions and continues the previous motion, which the adherence metric would show as a drop after round two.

TITLE: Bitwise vocabulary scaling for video tokens
PROPOSAL: We ask whether the bitwise prediction that lets Infinity grow its image vocabulary carries over to video tokens, where motion adds entropy. TITLE: Bitwise vocabulary scaling for video tokens
PROPOSAL: We ask whether the bitwise prediction that lets Infinity grow its image vocabulary carries over to video tokens, where motion adds entropy. TITLE: Image-to-video and extrapolation as prefix conditioning
PROPOSAL: We test whether a next-scale video model trained only on text-to-video can perform image-to-video and video extrapolation by placing the tokens of the given image or clip in the context as already generated frames, with no new training, and then whether a short fine-tuning on mixed tasks closes any remaining gap. TITLE: Spatiotemporal attention patterns that keep long contexts affordable
PROPOSAL: We replace full attention in the video generator with structured patterns and measure quality against context length: within-frame full attention plus attention to the same spatial block in previous frames, attention to previous frames only at the coarsest scale, and a learned selection of the most relevant previous-frame tokens per query. We report FVD, temporal flicker, and the attention operations per generated frame.
COST: 1300
PREDICTION: The block-local pattern with a coarse-scale link should hold FVD within a few points of full attention at a fraction of its attention operations on long clips, and the learned selection should gain at longer lengths but lose at training length. Flicker rising sharply beyond training length would mean that none of the patterns generalises temporally.

Problem statement:
Visual synthesis has witnessed remarkable progress in recent years, largely propelled by the scaling of Transformer architectures. Video generation in particular has attracted growing interest from both academia and industry, owing to its wide-ranging applications in content creation, world simulation and beyond. At present, diffusion models lead the field by iteratively denoising latent representations to produce high-fidelity clips. Concurrently, autoregressive models have been explored for their potential to unify image and video generation and to generalize over longer time horizons.

Despite their successes, each paradigm exhibits critical shortcomings. Video diffusion models excel at synthesizing fixed-length frame sequences by exploiting bidirectional attention, yet they incur substantial computational cost due to tens or even hundreds of sequential denoising steps, and they struggle to extend seamlessly to video extrapolation; their slow generation speed hinders the production of high-resolution, long-duration videos. Autoregressive methods based on next-token prediction, which predict video tokens in a fixed order (for example token by token along both spatial and temporal axes, as in Emu3, or set by set in space and then frame by frame in time, as in Nova), are inherently capable of streaming generation, but they often fall short in visual fidelity and require hundreds to tens of thousands of inference steps, resulting in prohibitive latency.

These observations motivate the need for a generation framework that simultaneously possesses high visual quality, efficiency and temporal generalization. In image synthesis, Visual AutoRegressive modeling (VAR) recently redefined generation as a coarse-to-fine next-scale prediction, and its follow-up, Infinity, introduced bitwise modeling and scaled up the vocabulary size, achieving performance comparable to diffusion models while offering significant advantages in inference speed. These advances, however, concern the spatial-only generation of static images. Whether a discrete autoregressive approach can deliver comparable quality and speed for video, where the temporal dimension, far larger token counts and the need for coherent motion come into play, remains an open question.

Several obstacles make this difficult. Discrete video tokenizers, on which purely discrete generators depend, are usually either trained from scratch, which is computationally heavy for clips of tens of frames and converges slowly, or initialized from discrete image tokenizers, whose weights are not optimal for video reconstruction. Long videos also imply long contexts: maintaining temporal consistency requires attending to previously generated content, yet attending to the full history leads to explosively long sequences and high computational cost.

The problem is therefore to design a single, purely discrete autoregressive model that generates high-resolution (e.g., 720p) videos with visual quality competitive with leading diffusion models at much lower inference latency, while unifying text-to-image, text-to-video, image-to-video and video extrapolation within one framework, and extending to long, multi-round video generation that follows successive user instructions. How should the temporal dimension be modeled so that a single model serves both images and videos and faithfully captures both appearance and motion? How can discrete video tokenizers with high reconstruction quality be obtained without prohibitive training cost? And how can the cost of long spatiotemporal contexts be contained without sacrificing temporal consistency or visual quality?

Paper type: Experimental only
Data type: Mostly real-world data
Experimental domains: text-to-video generation, text-to-image generation, image-to-video generation, video extrapolation, long interactive video generation

Problem statement:
Large language models (LLMs) can acquire new factual knowledge through fine-tuning, but the way they use such newly injected knowledge is puzzling. On the one hand, recent work showed that LLMs are able to deduce implications from learned facts: a model that learns the new fact "Alice lives in Paris" during fine-tuning can generalize at test time to deduce "Alice speaks French", an implication of the injected fact given that people living in Paris speak French. This indicates strong generalization capabilities. On the other hand, other work shows that LLMs tend to hallucinate factually incorrect responses when they learn new factual knowledge during fine-tuning. It remains unclear why LLMs can be good at generalization yet prone to hallucination after being injected with new factual knowledge. This raises a natural question: do generalization and hallucination on newly injected factual knowledge arise from the same underlying mechanism?

A capability closely related to this question is out-of-context reasoning, also referred to as "ripple effects": a model's ability to deduce implications beyond the explicitly trained knowledge by drawing connections between different pieces of knowledge. Prior studies of this capability in LLMs paint a mixed picture. Negative results have been reported on certain out-of-context reasoning tasks, such as the reversal curse and multi-hop in-weight reasoning, while other work shows that LLMs can associate two events when several subjects are involved in both events in the training data. Formally, atomic knowledge can be written as triples (s, r, a), where s is a subject, r a relation and a an answer. An underlying rule may link facts to implications, so that any subject s having relation r_1 with answer b_i also has relation r_2 with answer c_i; for example, (s, lives in, Paris) implies (s, speaks, French). Suppose a model is trained on data in which some subjects appear in both a fact and its corresponding implication. If a new subject appears during training only in the fact, can the model deduce the unseen implication at test time? And how, if at all, does this capability relate to the hallucinations observed after knowledge injection?

A rigorous understanding of this behavior is still lacking. The mechanism by which LLMs associate such events has so far been analyzed only empirically. A growing body of theoretical work explains how transformers acquire reasoning behaviors, such as induction heads, factual recall, the reversal curse, chain-of-thought reasoning and in-context two-hop reasoning, by studying their training dynamics. Yet it is not understood how gradient-based training leads a transformer to infer implications for subjects whose implications were never observed, which properties of the model and of its training make this possible, and under which conditions on the training data it occurs. Answering these questions would help explain both the strong generalization of LLMs after knowledge injection and their tendency to hallucinate, and could make it possible to predict when hallucination arises as new factual knowledge is injected into a model.

Paper type: Mostly theoretical
Data type: Mostly synthetic data
Experimental domains: factual knowledge injection in LLMs, open-domain question answering

TITLE: Out-of-context implication deduction as a function of bridging subjects
PROPOSAL: We build a synthetic corpus of triples where each subject has a fact relation r1 with answer b and, for a fraction of subjects, the implied relation r2 with answer c under a fixed rule from b to c. We train a two-layer transformer with learned embeddings from scratch on the corpus and test whether subjects seen only in the fact receive the correct implication, sweeping the fraction of bridging subjects from 0 to 0.5 and the number of rules from 1 to 50.
CONTROLS: A one-layer attention-only model, a bag-of-words model that cannot bind subject and relation, a corpus where the rule is broken by random c assignments, and a baseline that predicts the most frequent c. We report implication accuracy on held-out subjects and the rate of answers taken from the wrong rule, over three seeds.
COST: 40
PREDICTION: Implication accuracy should rise sharply once a small fraction of bridging subjects is present and then saturate, with the one-layer model staying near chance. If the broken-rule corpus gives the same accuracy, the model is exploiting answer frequency rather than deducing.

TITLE: One associative weight behind generalisation and hallucination after knowledge injection

TITLE: Training dynamics of implication transfer in a simplified transformer
PROPOSAL: We analyse gradient flow for a one-layer transformer with a single attention head followed by a two-layer MLP, trained with cross-entropy on synthetic triples under a rule from r1 answers to r2 answers, with orthogonal subject embeddings. We aim to prove that the MLP learns a map from the b answer direction to the c answer direction that is shared across subjects, and that this map transfers to a subject trained only on its r1 fact because the attention head writes the subject's b direction into the residual stream at the r2 query. We derive the time at which transfer appears as a function of the number of bridging subjects and the embedding dimension.
CONTROLS: Numerical simulation of the same model at dimensions 64, 256 and 1024 to check the predicted transfer time, a model without the MLP that should fail to transfer, and a 125M model trained on the same corpus to see whether the derived scaling holds beyond the simplified setting.
COST: 24
PREDICTION: Transfer time should scale inversely with the number of bridging subjects and the simulation should match the theory within a constant factor. The theory could fail if the attention head learns a subject-specific rather than a relation-level pattern, which the 125M model would reveal.

TITLE: Knowledge injection into pretrained models: deduction and hallucination on fictional entities

TITLE: Data conditions under which implication transfer appears
PROPOSAL: We map the region of training-data parameters in which a transformer trained from scratch on synthetic triples deduces unseen implications: the number of bridging subjects per rule, the number of distinct answers b, the ratio of fact to implication sentences, and the share of rule-violating subjects. Problem statement:
Large language models (LLMs) can acquire new factual knowledge through fine-tuning, but the way they use such newly injected knowledge is puzzling. On the one hand, recent work showed that LLMs are able to deduce implications from learned facts: a model that learns the new fact "Alice lives in Paris" during fine-tuning can generalize at test time to deduce "Alice speaks French", an implication of the injected fact given that people living in Paris speak French. This indicates strong generalization capabilities. On the other hand, other work shows that LLMs tend to hallucinate factually incorrect responses when they learn new factual knowledge during fine-tuning. It remains unclear why LLMs can be good at generalization yet prone to hallucination after being injected with new factual knowledge. This raises a natural question: do generalization and hallucination on newly injected factual knowledge arise from the same underlying mechanism?

A capability closely related to this question is out-of-context reasoning, also referred to as "ripple effects": a model's ability to deduce implications beyond the explicitly trained knowledge by drawing connections between different pieces of knowledge. Prior studies of this capability in LLMs paint a mixed picture. Negative results have been reported on certain out-of-context reasoning tasks, such as the reversal curse and multi-hop in-weight reasoning, while other work shows that LLMs can associate two events when several subjects are involved in both events in the training data. Formally, atomic knowledge can be written as triples (s, r, a), where s is a subject, r a relation and a an answer. An underlying rule may link facts to implications, so that any subject s having relation r_1 with answer b_i also has relation r_2 with answer c_i; for example, (s, lives in, Paris) implies (s, speaks, French). Suppose a model is trained on data in which some subjects appear in both a fact and its corresponding implication. If a new subject appears during training only in the fact, can the model deduce the unseen implication at test time? And how, if at all, does this capability relate to the hallucinations observed after knowledge injection?

A rigorous understanding of this behavior is still lacking. The mechanism by which LLMs associate such events has so far been analyzed only empirically. A growing body of theoretical work explains how transformers acquire reasoning behaviors, such as induction heads, factual recall, the reversal curse, chain-of-thought reasoning and in-context two-hop reasoning, by studying their training dynamics. Yet it is not understood how gradient-based training leads a transformer to infer implications for subjects whose implications were never observed, which properties of the model and of its training make this possible, and under which conditions on the training data it occurs. Answering these questions would help explain both the strong generalization of LLMs after knowledge injection and their tendency to hallucinate, and could make it possible to predict when hallucination arises as new factual knowledge is injected into a model.

Paper type: Mostly theoretical
Data type: Mostly synthetic data
Experimental domains: factual knowledge injection in LLMs, open-domain question answering

TITLE: Why implications transfer but reversals do not
PROPOSAL: We train the same two-layer transformer on two synthetic corpora, one where a rule links r1 answers to r2 answers for the same subject and one where the test requires answering the reversed relation from answer to subject, and we trace the attention and MLP pathways to explain why the first generalises for new subjects and the second does not. TITLE: Scaling of implication transfer with width, depth and data
PROPOSAL: Train transformers of 10M, 30M, 100M and 300M parameters from scratch on synthetic triples with ten rules and measure, for each, the number of bridging subjects needed before held-out implications are deduced, along with the hallucination rate on subjects whose fact lies outside every rule. Vary width at fixed depth and depth at fixed width to tell which dimension drives the threshold.
CONTROLS: A one-layer model at each width as the floor, a corpus with the rule removed, a memorisation baseline from co-occurrence counts, and three seeds per size with the threshold fitted per seed.
COST: 200
PREDICTION: The threshold of bridging subjects should fall with width but barely with depth, while the hallucination rate at threshold should stay nearly constant across sizes. If depth matters more, the mechanism needs composition across layers rather than a single map.

TITLE: In-weight against in-context deduction of implications
PROPOSAL: We compare two routes to the implication for a new subject: placing its fact in the prompt, or fine-tuning the fact into the weights, on the same two-layer transformer pretrained on synthetic triples with rules, and on Pythia-1.4B with fictional-person facts. Problem statement:
Depth estimation plays a pivotal role in 3D vision, enabling applications ranging from 3D reconstruction to augmented reality and robotics. Among the available techniques, Depth-from-Focus (DFF), also known as shape-from-focus, offers a passive, hardware-free approach that relies on a focal stack, a series of images of the same scene captured at different focal distances. This makes it particularly attractive for consumer-grade imaging systems such as smartphone cameras, which often lack dedicated stereo or depth sensors and must infer depth from limited inputs such as a single image or a focal sweep.

Unlike monocular or stereo depth estimation, DFF is grounded in a simple yet robust physical principle: a scene point appears sharpest when the camera's focal plane aligns with its depth, while points outside the depth of field are blurred into a circle of confusion. This focus-sharpness relationship provides an interpretable signal that, with proper calibration, can yield accurate metric depth. DFF is also inherently free from the scale ambiguity that affects monocular depth estimation, and it does not require scene-specific priors or extensive supervision. Classical DFF techniques nevertheless suffer from critical limitations. They search for the frame in which each pixel is maximally sharp using heuristic focus measures (for example Laplacian-based or frequency-domain contrast and sharpness operators) and then apply post-hoc smoothing to infer depth. They often require densely sampled stacks, are sensitive to noise in low-texture regions, and falter in the presence of ambiguous focus responses, fine textures or abrupt depth changes, producing depth maps that are either too blurry or riddled with noise.

Learning-based DFF methods have tackled some of these issues by training deep networks to learn focus patterns implicitly from data, including end-to-end convolutional networks trained on focal stacks, networks that produce intermediate defocus maps, self-supervised models that jointly reconstruct depth and all-in-focus images through a learned defocus simulation, networks that exploit differences of features across focal planes, and hybrid models that refine pretrained relative-depth predictions into metric depth with a DFF backbone. While these models achieve notable improvements in benchmark performance, they tend to treat focal-stack images much like ordinary all-in-focus frames and to infer depth directly from appearance features. They typically overlook the underlying physical and geometric principles of focusing, such as the gradual changes in sharpness driven by the focus behavior of light in a camera, and they remain vulnerable to texture-induced artifacts: a strong image gradient may come from a surface texture or a repeating pattern rather than from a genuine depth discontinuity. In particular, they do not fully exploit the complementary roles of spatial information (how structure varies between neighboring pixels) and focal information (how focus evolves across the slices of the stack), which are essential for accurate and robust DFF in complex real-world scenes. Spatial regularization and gradient-based priors have benefited depth estimation more broadly, but they were developed for single-image or generic depth settings, without access to the multi-focus information that a focal stack provides.

The open problem is therefore how a learning-based DFF model can take into account the physics of focus and the distinctive structure of focal stacks, along both their spatial and focal dimensions, rather than treating them as generic images. How can such a model (i) distinguish true depth edges from texture-induced gradients, (ii) disambiguate noisy or misleading focus cues, including in fine-textured, low-texture or reflective regions and at abrupt depth changes, and (iii) produce depth maps that are both accurate and sharp without being noisy, while remaining robust across diverse real-world scenes?

Data type: Mostly real-world data
Experimental domains: depth from focus (focal-stack depth estimation), indoor scene depth estimation

TITLE: Sparse stacks and noisy slices as a stress test for physics-aware focus models
PROPOSAL: We ask whether a model that reads the stack along its focal axis stays accurate when the stack becomes sparse. We build a network whose first stage fits, per pixel, a parametric sharpness curve across slices using the thin-lens relation between depth and circle of confusion (CoC) diameter, and whose second stage refines the curve parameters spatially with an edge-aware convolutional neural network (CNN). We train on the Focus-on-Defocus benchmark (FoD500) and on focal stacks rendered from the New York University Depth version two dataset (NYU Depth v2), then evaluate with stacks subsampled to a quarter of their slices and with added sensor noise.
CONTROLS: DefocusNet and a deep focus volume network retrained under the same subsampling, a Laplacian focus measure with guided filtering, our model with the parametric stage replaced by a free per-pixel argmax, and the full stack as an upper reference, reported as root mean square error (RMSE) and absolute relative error on all pixels and on depth-edge pixels.
COST: 280
PREDICTION: The parametric curve should degrade gracefully as slices are removed, while the argmax variant and the learned baselines should lose accuracy sharply below eight slices. Gains may vanish on reflective regions where no single sharpness peak exists.
