Problem statement:
Depth estimation plays a pivotal role in 3D vision, enabling applications ranging from 3D reconstruction to augmented reality and robotics. Among the available techniques, Depth-from-Focus (DFF), also known as shape-from-focus, offers a passive, hardware-free approach that relies on a focal stack, a series of images of the same scene captured at different focal distances. This makes it particularly attractive for consumer-grade imaging systems such as smartphone cameras, which often lack dedicated stereo or depth sensors and must infer depth from limited inputs such as a single image or a focal sweep.

Unlike monocular or stereo depth estimation, DFF is grounded in a simple yet robust physical principle: a scene point appears sharpest when the camera's focal plane aligns with its depth, while points outside the depth of field are blurred into a circle of confusion. This focus-sharpness relationship provides an interpretable signal that, with proper calibration, can yield accurate metric depth. DFF is also inherently free from the scale ambiguity that affects monocular depth estimation, and it does not require scene-specific priors or extensive supervision. Classical DFF techniques nevertheless suffer from critical limitations. They search for the frame in which each pixel is maximally sharp using heuristic focus measures (for example Laplacian-based or frequency-domain contrast and sharpness operators) and then apply post-hoc smoothing to infer depth. They often require densely sampled stacks, are sensitive to noise in low-texture regions, and falter in the presence of ambiguous focus responses, fine textures or abrupt depth changes, producing depth maps that are either too blurry or riddled with noise.

Learning-based DFF methods have tackled some of these issues by training deep networks to learn focus patterns implicitly from data, including end-to-end convolutional networks trained on focal stacks, networks that produce intermediate defocus maps, self-supervised models that jointly reconstruct depth and all-in-focus images through a learned defocus simulation, networks that exploit differences of features across focal planes, and hybrid models that refine pretrained relative-depth predictions into metric depth with a DFF backbone. While these models achieve notable improvements in benchmark performance, they tend to treat focal-stack images much like ordinary all-in-focus frames and to infer depth directly from appearance features. They typically overlook the underlying physical and geometric principles of focusing, such as the gradual changes in sharpness driven by the focus behavior of light in a camera, and they remain vulnerable to texture-induced artifacts: a strong image gradient may come from a surface texture or a repeating pattern rather than from a genuine depth discontinuity. In particular, they do not fully exploit the complementary roles of spatial information (how structure varies between neighboring pixels) and focal information (how focus evolves across the slices of the stack), which are essential for accurate and robust DFF in complex real-world scenes. Spatial regularization and gradient-based priors have benefited depth estimation more broadly, but they were developed for single-image or generic depth settings, without access to the multi-focus information that a focal stack provides.

The open problem is therefore how a learning-based DFF model can take into account the physics of focus and the distinctive structure of focal stacks, along both their spatial and focal dimensions, rather than treating them as generic images. How can such a model (i) distinguish true depth edges from texture-induced gradients, (ii) disambiguate noisy or misleading focus cues, including in fine-textured, low-texture or reflective regions and at abrupt depth changes, and (iii) produce depth maps that are both accurate and sharp without being noisy, while remaining robust across diverse real-world scenes?

Paper type: Mostly experimental
Data type: Mostly real-world data
Experimental domains: depth from focus (focal-stack depth estimation), indoor scene depth estimation

TITLE: Focal-axis attention versus 3D convolution for focal-stack depth
PROPOSAL: We compare two ways of reading the focal dimension: a transformer that attends across slices at each spatial location before a spatial decoder, and a 3D convolutional encoder that mixes spatial and focal axes jointly. Both receive the same per-slice features and the slice focus distances as positional codes. We train both on DDFF-12-Scene and on synthetic stacks rendered from NYU Depth v2 with a thin-lens blur, and test on FoD500 and on real smartphone sweeps with stacks of varying length.
CONTROLS: DefocusNet and DFV as published designs retrained on our splits, a per-slice 2D encoder with max pooling over slices, the focal transformer with shuffled slice order to test whether it uses the focal structure, and a classical Laplacian focus measure with guided filter smoothing, with three seeds per configuration.
COST: 360
PREDICTION: The focal transformer should generalise better to stacks of lengths unseen in training than the 3D convolutional encoder, and both should beat the pooled 2D encoder on abrupt depth changes. If shuffling the slice order costs nothing, the model reads appearance rather than focus evolution.

TITLE: Cross-dataset transfer of focal-stack depth under camera changes
PROPOSAL: We test whether a depth-from-focus model that takes the calibrated focus distances and aperture as input transfers across cameras. We train a network that normalises each slice's focus distance by the camera's hyperfocal distance and predicts depth in units of the circle-of-confusion scale, then converts to metric depth with the calibration. Training uses DDFF-12-Scene, and we evaluate zero-shot on FoD500 and on the Mobile Depth dataset, which come from different lenses, before and after fine-tuning on a small subset of each.
CONTROLS: The same network without calibration inputs, DDFFNet and AiFDepthNet trained identically, a monocular relative-depth model aligned to ground truth by least squares as a scale-free comparison, and a classical focus measure with per-camera depth lookup. We report RMSE, absolute relative error and the ratio of errors before and after fine-tuning.
COST: 300
PREDICTION: Calibration-aware prediction should transfer with far less loss than the uncalibrated network, whose errors should scale with the mismatch in aperture between cameras. We may see no benefit on the Mobile Depth dataset if its calibration metadata is too coarse.

TITLE: Synthetic focal stacks with controlled texture to isolate texture-induced depth errors
PROPOSAL: We render focal stacks from NYU Depth v2 and from procedurally generated scenes where we control, per surface, the texture frequency, the presence of repeating patterns and the sharpness of depth discontinuities, using a thin-lens blur with a calibrated circle of confusion. We train a depth network on this data with a loss that weights depth-gradient errors by the mismatch between image gradients and ground-truth depth gradients, so that the model learns to discount gradients that do not correspond to depth. We then evaluate on real DDFF-12-Scene and FoD500 stacks.
CONTROLS: Training on the same renders with an unweighted L1 loss, DefocusNet and DFV trained on the same renders, a classical sum-of-modified-Laplacian pipeline, and an evaluation split of real scenes with high-frequency textures on flat surfaces, scored by RMSE and by the number of spurious depth edges found by a Canny detector on the depth map.
COST: 220
PREDICTION: The gradient-mismatch weighting should reduce spurious depth edges on textured flat surfaces by a wide factor while leaving RMSE on true edges unchanged. The gain may not transfer to real stacks if the synthetic blur differs from real lens behaviour.

TITLE: Synthetic focal stacks with controlled texture to isolate texture-induced depth errors
PROPOSAL: We render focal stacks from NYU Depth v2 and from procedurally generated scenes where we control, per surface, the texture frequency, the presence of repeating patterns and the sharpness of depth discontinuities, using a thin-lens blur with a calibrated circle of confusion. Problem statement:
Depth estimation plays a pivotal role in 3D vision, enabling applications ranging from 3D reconstruction to augmented reality and robotics. Among the available techniques, Depth-from-Focus (DFF), also known as shape-from-focus, offers a passive, hardware-free approach that relies on a focal stack, a series of images of the same scene captured at different focal distances. This makes it particularly attractive for consumer-grade imaging systems such as smartphone cameras, which often lack dedicated stereo or depth sensors and must infer depth from limited inputs such as a single image or a focal sweep.

Unlike monocular or stereo depth estimation, DFF is grounded in a simple yet robust physical principle: a scene point appears sharpest when the camera's focal plane aligns with its depth, while points outside the depth of field are blurred into a circle of confusion. This focus-sharpness relationship provides an interpretable signal that, with proper calibration, can yield accurate metric depth. DFF is also inherently free from the scale ambiguity that affects monocular depth estimation, and it does not require scene-specific priors or extensive supervision. Classical DFF techniques nevertheless suffer from critical limitations. They search for the frame in which each pixel is maximally sharp using heuristic focus measures (for example Laplacian-based or frequency-domain contrast and sharpness operators) and then apply post-hoc smoothing to infer depth. They often require densely sampled stacks, are sensitive to noise in low-texture regions, and falter in the presence of ambiguous focus responses, fine textures or abrupt depth changes, producing depth maps that are either too blurry or riddled with noise.

Learning-based DFF methods have tackled some of these issues by training deep networks to learn focus patterns implicitly from data, including end-to-end convolutional networks trained on focal stacks, networks that produce intermediate defocus maps, self-supervised models that jointly reconstruct depth and all-in-focus images through a learned defocus simulation, networks that exploit differences of features across focal planes, and hybrid models that refine pretrained relative-depth predictions into metric depth with a DFF backbone. While these models achieve notable improvements in benchmark performance, they tend to treat focal-stack images much like ordinary all-in-focus frames and to infer depth directly from appearance features. They typically overlook the underlying physical and geometric principles of focusing, such as the gradual changes in sharpness driven by the focus behavior of light in a camera, and they remain vulnerable to texture-induced artifacts: a strong image gradient may come from a surface texture or a repeating pattern rather than from a genuine depth discontinuity. In particular, they do not fully exploit the complementary roles of spatial information (how structure varies between neighboring pixels) and focal information (how focus evolves across the slices of the stack), which are essential for accurate and robust DFF in complex real-world scenes. Spatial regularization and gradient-based priors have benefited depth estimation more broadly, but they were developed for single-image or generic depth settings, without access to the multi-focus information that a focal stack provides.

The open problem is therefore how a learning-based DFF model can take into account the physics of focus and the distinctive structure of focal stacks, along both their spatial and focal dimensions, rather than treating them as generic images. How can such a model (i) distinguish true depth edges from texture-induced gradients, (ii) disambiguate noisy or misleading focus cues, including in fine-textured, low-texture or reflective regions and at abrupt depth changes, and (iii) produce depth maps that are both accurate and sharp without being noisy, while remaining robust across diverse real-world scenes?

TITLE: Joint depth and all-in-focus estimation with sharpness consistency
PROPOSAL: We train a network that outputs depth and an all-in-focus image together and enforce consistency between them: the all-in-focus image, blurred at each pixel according to the predicted depth and each slice's focus distance, must reproduce the input stack, and the sharpness of the all-in-focus image must exceed that of every slice at every pixel. The second constraint penalises depth estimates that pick a slice where the scene point is still blurred, which happens in low-texture regions. Training uses DDFF-12-Scene with labels and unlabelled 4D Light Field stacks, with evaluation on FoD500.
CONTROLS: AiFDepthNet, which also reconstructs the stack but without the sharpness constraint, DefocusNet trained with labels only, the same network trained without the sharpness term, and a classical focus measure with guided filter smoothing. We report RMSE, absolute relative error, and a boundary error on depth edges.
COST: 340
PREDICTION: The sharpness constraint should reduce errors in low-texture regions where the reconstruction loss alone is nearly flat in depth. If the term brings no gain over AiFDepthNet retrained on our data, the reconstruction loss already captures it.

TITLE: Noise-aware focus volumes for sharp, clean depth maps
PROPOSAL: We build a focus volume whose per-slice sharpness is computed by a learned operator trained to be invariant to sensor noise, using pairs of clean and noise-augmented stacks, and we decode depth from this volume with a cost-volume style soft argmax followed by a learned edge-preserving filter that takes the all-in-focus image as guidance. Training uses DDFF-12-Scene and FoD500 with photometric noise augmentation, and we evaluate on real stacks captured in low light with the Mobile Depth dataset and our own additions.
CONTROLS: DFV with its fixed Laplacian focus volume, DDFFNet, a classical focus measure with and without denoising applied to the slices beforehand, and our model with the learned operator swapped for a Laplacian, evaluated at several noise levels by RMSE and by a measure of speckle in flat regions.
COST: 200
PREDICTION: The learned operator should keep RMSE nearly flat as noise rises, while the Laplacian-based volumes degrade quickly. If denoising the slices first closes the gap, a learned operator is not needed.

Problem statement:
Diffusion models have made substantial advances in visual synthesis. Driven by the growing demand for higher fidelity and quality, research has focused on scaling up diffusion models, which has propelled an architectural shift from U-Net backbones to the now-prevalent Diffusion Transformers (DiTs). Despite the proven effectiveness of DiT-based models, their dense activation of all parameters, irrespective of task or input, incurs substantial computational overhead and hinders further scaling.

To scale toward larger and more capable models, the large language model (LLM) community has widely adopted the Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) paradigm, which expands model capacity while maintaining computational efficiency. An MoE layer dispatches each input token to a few specialized "expert" sub-networks (typically feed-forward networks) via a learned router and returns a weighted sum of the selected experts' outputs, so that only a fraction of the parameters is activated for each token. Despite MoE's profound success in language modeling, recent efforts to bring it to DiTs have not yielded the significant gains observed in LLMs. Early MoE variants for U-Net-based diffusion models mostly assigned experts by ranges of diffusion timesteps. For DiTs, DiT-MoE, which uses token-choice routing (each token selects its top experts), often underperforms dense counterparts despite activating the same number of parameters; EC-DiT, which uses expert-choice routing (each expert takes a fixed quota of tokens), delivers only marginal gains even with extended training; and DiffMoE, which routes tokens through a batch-level global token-distribution scheme, still reports relatively limited improvements. This pronounced gap between MoE's transformative impact in LLMs and its modest returns in DiTs motivates a fundamental question: what are the underlying factors that impede the effectiveness of MoE in DiT models?

A foundational principle of MoE design is expert specialization: each expert should acquire focused, non-overlapping knowledge, consistently processing similar patterns, while different experts take on distinct functions. In language modeling, discrete text tokens are semantically dense and clearly distinguishable from one another, which provides a strong inductive bias that naturally fosters such specialization. The tokens processed by a DiT are of a different nature: they are patches of a continuous image latent processed by a denoising network. It is not known whether such tokens offer a comparable basis for specialization, nor which of their properties prevent current routers from learning distinct experts. The problem is therefore twofold: to identify how visual tokens in diffusion transformers differ from language tokens in ways that matter for routing and expert specialization, and to determine how the routing of an MoE should be designed for DiTs so that experts become genuinely specialized, allowing MoE to improve generation quality over dense DiTs at the same number of activated parameters and to keep doing so as model size and the number of experts grow.

PROPOSAL: We train DiT-B/2 with token-choice MoE layers of eight experts on ImageNet at 256 resolution and record, for every latent patch, the expert chosen at each layer across denoising timesteps, across neighbouring patches, and across samples of the same class. Problem statement:
Diffusion models have made substantial advances in visual synthesis. Driven by the growing demand for higher fidelity and quality, research has focused on scaling up diffusion models, which has propelled an architectural shift from U-Net backbones to the now-prevalent Diffusion Transformers (DiTs). Despite the proven effectiveness of DiT-based models, their dense activation of all parameters, irrespective of task or input, incurs substantial computational overhead and hinders further scaling.

To scale toward larger and more capable models, the large language model (LLM) community has widely adopted the Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) paradigm, which expands model capacity while maintaining computational efficiency. An MoE layer dispatches each input token to a few specialized "expert" sub-networks (typically feed-forward networks) via a learned router and returns a weighted sum of the selected experts' outputs, so that only a fraction of the parameters is activated for each token. Despite MoE's profound success in language modeling, recent efforts to bring it to DiTs have not yielded the significant gains observed in LLMs. Early MoE variants for U-Net-based diffusion models mostly assigned experts by ranges of diffusion timesteps. For DiTs, DiT-MoE, which uses token-choice routing (each token selects its top experts), often underperforms dense counterparts despite activating the same number of parameters; EC-DiT, which uses expert-choice routing (each expert takes a fixed quota of tokens), delivers only marginal gains even with extended training; and DiffMoE, which routes tokens through a batch-level global token-distribution scheme, still reports relatively limited improvements. This pronounced gap between MoE's transformative impact in LLMs and its modest returns in DiTs motivates a fundamental question: what are the underlying factors that impede the effectiveness of MoE in DiT models?

A foundational principle of MoE design is expert specialization: each expert should acquire focused, non-overlapping knowledge, consistently processing similar patterns, while different experts take on distinct functions. In language modeling, discrete text tokens are semantically dense and clearly distinguishable from one another, which provides a strong inductive bias that naturally fosters such specialization. The tokens processed by a DiT are of a different nature: they are patches of a continuous image latent processed by a denoising network. It is not known whether such tokens offer a comparable basis for specialization, nor which of their properties prevent current routers from learning distinct experts. The problem is therefore twofold: to identify how visual tokens in diffusion transformers differ from language tokens in ways that matter for routing and expert specialization, and to determine how the routing of an MoE should be designed for DiTs so that experts become genuinely specialized, allowing MoE to improve generation quality over dense DiTs at the same number of activated parameters and to keep doing so as model size and the number of experts grow.

TITLE: Scaling experts and model size under a specialisation-promoting router
PROPOSAL: We test whether a router trained with an auxiliary loss that rewards non-overlapping expert inputs keeps improving over dense DiTs as the model and the number of experts grow. The loss pushes apart the mean input features of different experts and penalises tokens whose top two expert scores are close. CONTROLS: Dense models at each size, token-choice routing with the standard load-balancing loss only, expert-choice routing, a random fixed router, and all variants trained for equal numbers of samples with the same sampler and guidance scale.
COST: 3600
PREDICTION: The gap over dense should widen with model size and expert count for the specialisation loss, while token-choice routing should stay flat or shrink. If the random router scales equally well, capacity rather than routing explains the gains.

TITLE: Spatially coherent routing with neighbourhood-pooled router inputs
PROPOSAL: We feed the router not the single token but a pooled feature over its spatial neighbourhood and the timestep embedding, so that nearby patches of a continuous latent choose experts together, and we add a loss that rewards agreement between adjacent patches' assignments. PREDICTION: Coherent routing should reduce FID below token-choice routing and reach a clear gain over dense at both sizes, with the gain larger at DiT-L/2. If the content-free coherent router performs as well, coherence alone and not content drives the gain.

TITLE: Dense-to-MoE upcycling with expert initialisation from feature clusters
PROPOSAL: We start from a trained dense DiT-XL/2 and convert each feed-forward block into eight experts initialised from the dense weights, but we initialise the router from k-means centroids of token features recorded from the dense model at several timesteps, so that experts start with distinct input regions. COST: 3000
PREDICTION: Cluster-initialised routers should keep their partition and beat the dense continuation in FID, while random routers should drift towards uniform assignments. If the shuffled-centroid placebo does equally well, the initial partition does not matter.

Problem statement:
Diffusion models have made substantial advances in visual synthesis. Driven by the growing demand for higher fidelity and quality, research has focused on scaling up diffusion models, which has propelled an architectural shift from U-Net backbones to the now-prevalent Diffusion Transformers (DiTs). Despite the proven effectiveness of DiT-based models, their dense activation of all parameters, irrespective of task or input, incurs substantial computational overhead and hinders further scaling.

To scale toward larger and more capable models, the large language model (LLM) community has widely adopted the Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) paradigm, which expands model capacity while maintaining computational efficiency. An MoE layer dispatches each input token to a few specialized "expert" sub-networks (typically feed-forward networks) via a learned router and returns a weighted sum of the selected experts' outputs, so that only a fraction of the parameters is activated for each token. Despite MoE's profound success in language modeling, recent efforts to bring it to DiTs have not yielded the significant gains observed in LLMs. Early MoE variants for U-Net-based diffusion models mostly assigned experts by ranges of diffusion timesteps. For DiTs, DiT-MoE, which uses token-choice routing (each token selects its top experts), often underperforms dense counterparts despite activating the same number of parameters; EC-DiT, which uses expert-choice routing (each expert takes a fixed quota of tokens), delivers only marginal gains even with extended training; and DiffMoE, which routes tokens through a batch-level global token-distribution scheme, still reports relatively limited improvements. This pronounced gap between MoE's transformative impact in LLMs and its modest returns in DiTs motivates a fundamental question: what are the underlying factors that impede the effectiveness of MoE in DiT models?

A foundational principle of MoE design is expert specialization: each expert should acquire focused, non-overlapping knowledge, consistently processing similar patterns, while different experts take on distinct functions. In language modeling, discrete text tokens are semantically dense and clearly distinguishable from one another, which provides a strong inductive bias that naturally fosters such specialization. The tokens processed by a DiT are of a different nature: they are patches of a continuous image latent processed by a denoising network. It is not known whether such tokens offer a comparable basis for specialization, nor which of their properties prevent current routers from learning distinct experts. The problem is therefore twofold: to identify how visual tokens in diffusion transformers differ from language tokens in ways that matter for routing and expert specialization, and to determine how the routing of an MoE should be designed for DiTs so that experts become genuinely specialized, allowing MoE to improve generation quality over dense DiTs at the same number of activated parameters and to keep doing so as model size and the number of experts grow.

TITLE: Load balancing versus specialisation in diffusion transformer experts
PROPOSAL: We test whether the standard load-balancing loss, borrowed from language MoE, is what prevents experts in DiTs from specialising. We train DiT-B/2 with eight experts and token-choice routing on ImageNet at 256 resolution with the balancing weight swept across a range down to zero, with a capacity-based alternative that drops tokens instead of penalising imbalance, and with a loss that balances only within each timestep bucket. We measure FID, expert utilisation, the overlap of expert input sets and the consistency of assignments across timesteps, keeping activated parameters equal to the dense model.
CONTROLS: Dense DiT-B/2, EC-DiT and DiffMoE under the same schedule and sampler, a random router at each balancing weight, and three seeds for the two extreme weights.
COST: 1800
PREDICTION: Lower balancing weights should raise specialisation and FID gain until expert collapse sets in, and per-timestep balancing should keep utilisation high without harming specialisation. If FID is flat across weights, balancing is not the obstacle.

Problem statement:
Offline reinforcement learning (RL) trains policies from static, pre-collected datasets, avoiding costly or risky online interaction when gathering additional data is infeasible. Yet agents trained on fully observable states often fail when deployed with noisy or corrupted observations. Test-time robust offline RL methods train on a clean, stationary dataset and are then evaluated under perturbed observations, but the perturbations they consider are synthetic ones such as sensor noise or adversarial attacks; other offline RL methods typically assume stationarity altogether. These assumptions often fail in real-world scenarios characterized by abrupt, time-varying shifts, and a critical gap persists in addressing non-stationarity within the observation function, which fundamentally alters the agent's perception of the environment over time. Research on non-stationary RL has predominantly focused on evolving transition dynamics and reward functions. Meta-learning approaches to online adaptation often require samples from the current environment and struggle with non-trivial non-stationarity, while future-oriented methods that anticipate how the environment will evolve assume fully observable states at test time and online interaction during training. Prior online algorithms that treat the observation function as the scope of non-stationarity have focused on learning agent morphologies and on generalization in Block MDPs; despite its significant potential for real-world applications, this scope of non-stationarity remains underexplored.

The setting of interest is the episodic evolution of the observation function at test time in offline RL. During training, only a standard offline RL dataset collected from a stationary environment with fully observable states is available; such data may have been gathered under near-ideal conditions, before wear, tear, or other natural shifts set in. At deployment, the state space, action space, transition dynamics, and reward function are unchanged, but each dimension of the agent's state is shifted by an unknown, time-dependent additive offset that remains fixed within an episode (a single operational interval) and changes across episodes, independently of the agent's actions and possibly differently for each dimension. This produces a temporally ordered stream of evolving observation functions, extending over many future episodes, during which the offsets remain hidden. For instance, industrial robots might apply a daily calibration offset to each joint, sensors can exhibit a deviation until the next scheduled recalibration, and in healthcare or finance data may be partially aggregated or withheld to comply with regulations, leaving a single offset as the dominant factor per episode. These offsets need not conform to Gaussian or Markovian assumptions: they may follow complex, abrupt, non-Markovian real-world time-series patterns. At most, the agent may receive a limited history of past offsets at discrete intervals, but never the offsets of the upcoming episodes, and in some deployments it may have no access to past offsets at all. Storing only such per-episode offset values, separately from massive interaction buffers, is attractive in bandwidth-constrained or privacy-sensitive environments.

This problem is challenging for several reasons. Each test episode is partially observable: for any single observation there are infinitely many pairs of state and offset that could have produced it, and since the initial state is drawn uniformly over the state space, it carries no information about the offset. An agent may thus know which environment it operates in but not where it actually is within it, and remain uncertain across all test episodes, as every new offset creates a systematic misalignment between perceived and actual states. Approaches that assume predefined perturbations struggle with such abrupt, episodic shifts, which violate the usual assumption of smoothly varying observation functions; standard noise-driven or parametric state-estimation techniques, which rely on smoothly varying or randomly perturbed functions, cannot reliably identify persistent, episode-wide offsets that are not revealed after the episode ends. Extrapolating past offsets into the future is itself error-prone for complex real-world series. Finally, frequent retraining, hyperparameter optimization, or extensive online adaptation to each new pattern of evolution is costly, risky in safety-critical settings because of trial and error, and may be infeasible when the new patterns no longer reflect the assumptions made during training.

The central question is therefore: how can an agent trained only on stationary, fully observable offline data act robustly, from the very onset of each episode, in an environment whose observations are shifted by hidden, time-varying, per-dimension additive offsets following arbitrary real-world time-series patterns, without interacting with the environment or knowing the partially observable test-time structure during training, without retraining or retuning when unseen patterns of non-stationarity appear, and without presupposing any specific pattern of future non-stationarity? Answering it would help bridge the gap between offline RL and the complexities of real-world, non-stationary environments.

TITLE: Acting on observation differences to cancel episode-constant offsets
PROPOSAL: An additive offset that stays fixed for a whole episode cancels exactly in the difference between two consecutive observations, so we train a policy whose inputs are the last eight observation differences and the last eight actions rather than the raw state. We use TD3+BC and IQL on the D4RL Hopper, Walker2d, HalfCheetah and AntMaze-medium datasets, rewriting every stored transition into difference form before training, with a gated recurrent encoder to recover velocity-like and phase-like information that the absolute state would otherwise carry. At test time each episode receives a per-dimension offset taken from real series: electricity-load, exchange-rate and sensor-drift records rescaled to twice the per-dimension standard deviation of the dataset. We report normalised return over two hundred ordered episodes and the fraction of the clean-observation return retained.

Meta-learning approaches to online adaptation often require samples from the current environment and struggle with non-trivial non-stationarity, while future-oriented methods that anticipate how the environment will evolve assume fully observable states at test time and online interaction during training. Prior online algorithms that treat the observation function as the scope of non-stationarity have focused on learning agent morphologies and on generalization in Block MDPs; despite its significant potential for real-world applications, this scope of non-stationarity remains underexplored.

TITLE: Estimating the episode offset from dynamics consistency during the episode
PROPOSAL: We learn an ensemble of forward dynamics models on the offline dataset and, at deployment, treat the unknown per-dimension offset as a parameter to be estimated from the transitions observed so far in the episode. After each step we solve a small least-squares problem that finds the offset vector under which the corrected transitions best agree with the learned dynamics, warm-started from the previous estimate, and we feed the corrected observation to a frozen IQL policy. Before the first estimate is available the policy acts on an offset-free guess. We evaluate on D4RL locomotion tasks and on Adroit pen and door manipulation, with offsets drawn from recorded calibration logs and from piecewise-constant jumps, and we report the return and the estimation error as a function of the step index within the episode.
CONTROLS: The frozen policy on uncorrected observations, the same policy given the exact offset, a Kalman filter that assumes Gaussian drift in the offset, the estimator run with a single dynamics model instead of the ensemble, and the estimator fed transitions from a different episode to check that it uses the current episode rather than a dataset prior.
COST: 260
PREDICTION: Estimation error should fall below the policy's tolerance within the first dozen steps on locomotion tasks, so that returns approach the exact-offset reference. On manipulation tasks whose dynamics barely move in early steps the estimate may stay ambiguous for longer and returns may remain closer to the uncorrected policy.

TITLE: Offset randomisation with a recurrent behaviour-regularised actor
PROPOSAL: We train a recurrent actor-critic with behaviour-cloning regularisation on standard offline locomotion and manipulation datasets, applying to every sampled trajectory a per-dimension additive offset held constant along the whole trajectory. Offsets come from a broad mixture of uniform, heavy-tailed and sparse vectors in which only a few dimensions move, so that the recurrent state learns to recognise the current offset from its first transitions rather than memorise one family of shifts. CONTROLS: The same recurrent actor trained without any offset, a feed-forward actor trained with the same offsets, the feed-forward actor on clean observations as an upper reference, and a variant in which training offsets are drawn from the same series family as the test stream, to measure how much is gained by matching the family.
COST: 450
PREDICTION: The recurrent actor trained on the broad mixture should recover most of the clean return within a handful of steps per episode and generalise to unseen series without retraining. Should the family-matched variant clearly dominate, the mixture is too narrow and the approach depends on knowing the pattern in advance.

Problem statement:

Yet agents trained on fully observable states often fail when deployed with noisy or corrupted observations. These assumptions often fail in real-world scenarios characterized by abrupt, time-varying shifts, and a critical gap persists in addressing non-stationarity within the observation function, which fundamentally alters the agent's perception of the environment over time. Research on non-stationary RL has predominantly focused on evolving transition dynamics and reward functions. Meta-learning approaches to online adaptation often require samples from the current environment and struggle with non-trivial non-stationarity, while future-oriented methods that anticipate how the environment will evolve assume fully observable states at test time and online interaction during training. Prior online algorithms that treat the observation function as the scope of non-stationarity have focused on learning agent morphologies and on generalization in Block MDPs; despite its significant potential for real-world applications, this scope of non-stationarity remains underexplored.

The setting of interest is the episodic evolution of the observation function at test time in offline RL. During training, only a standard offline RL dataset collected from a stationary environment with fully observable states is available; such data may have been gathered under near-ideal conditions, before wear, tear, or other natural shifts set in. At deployment, the state space, action space, transition dynamics, and reward function are unchanged, but each dimension of the agent's state is shifted by an unknown, time-dependent additive offset that remains fixed within an episode (a single operational interval) and changes across episodes, independently of the agent's actions and possibly differently for each dimension. This produces a temporally ordered stream of evolving observation functions, extending over many future episodes, during which the offsets remain hidden. For instance, industrial robots might apply a daily calibration offset to each joint, sensors can exhibit a deviation until the next scheduled recalibration, and in healthcare or finance data may be partially aggregated or withheld to comply with regulations, leaving a single offset as the dominant factor per episode. These offsets need not conform to Gaussian or Markovian assumptions: they may follow complex, abrupt, non-Markovian real-world time-series patterns. At most, the agent may receive a limited history of past offsets at discrete intervals, but never the offsets of the upcoming episodes, and in some deployments it may have no access to past offsets at all. Storing only such per-episode offset values, separately from massive interaction buffers, is attractive in bandwidth-constrained or privacy-sensitive environments.

This problem is challenging for several reasons. Each test episode is partially observable: for any single observation there are infinitely many pairs of state and offset that could have produced it, and since the initial state is drawn uniformly over the state space, it carries no information about the offset. An agent may thus know which environment it operates in but not where it actually is within it, and remain uncertain across all test episodes, as every new offset creates a systematic misalignment between perceived and actual states. Extrapolating past offsets into the future is itself error-prone for complex real-world series. Finally, frequent retraining, hyperparameter optimization, or extensive online adaptation to each new pattern of evolution is costly, risky in safety-critical settings because of trial and error, and may be infeasible when the new patterns no longer reflect the assumptions made during training.

TITLE: A benchmark of episodic observation offsets drawn from real series

TITLE: Pessimistic action selection over a posterior of offset hypotheses
PROPOSAL: We keep, during each test episode, a discrete set of candidate offset vectors per dimension on a grid centred on zero, and a weight for each candidate updated after every step from how well the corrected transition agrees with an ensemble of dynamics models learned offline. Actions are chosen to maximise the expected value of a frozen Q-function under the current weights minus a penalty on the spread of that value across candidates, which makes the agent cautious while the offset is still ambiguous and increasingly decisive as the weights concentrate. The Q-function and dynamics models are trained with conservative Q-learning on publicly released offline locomotion and manipulation datasets. Test streams use offsets following recorded series of sensor drift and abrupt recalibration steps, and we report return along the stream and the entropy of the candidate weights over the episode.
CONTROLS: The same Q-function acting on uncorrected observations, acting with the true offset, acting with the weighted mean candidate and no spread penalty, the weights frozen at uniform throughout the episode, and a finer and a coarser grid of candidates.
COST: 300
PREDICTION: The spread penalty should matter mainly in the first steps of each episode, after which the weighted-mean variant catches up. On tasks where early actions are irreversible, such as falling in Hopper, the penalty should give a clear gain over the weighted mean.

TITLE: Using a short history of past offsets as a prior for in-episode inference
PROPOSAL: We study the deployment variant in which the agent receives the offsets of a limited number of past episodes at discrete intervals, and we ask how much that history is worth once combined with in-episode inference. We fit a nonparametric prior over offsets, a kernel density on the last twenty recorded offsets per dimension, and use it to initialise a particle set that is then reweighted during the episode from the agreement of corrected transitions with a learned dynamics ensemble. The policy, trained with TD3+BC on D4RL Walker2d, HalfCheetah and Adroit relocate datasets, acts on the particle-weighted corrected observation. We evaluate on streams whose offsets follow three kinds of real series, slow drift, periodic recalibration and irregular jumps, and we report return against the number of past offsets provided, from none to twenty.
CONTROLS: Particles initialised uniformly without any history, the prior used alone without in-episode reweighting, a direct forecaster trained on the past offsets and used without correction, and the policy given the exact offset.
COST: 240
PREDICTION: History should help on slow drift and matter little on irregular jumps, where in-episode reweighting should carry the result. We expect the prior-only variant to fail on jumps, which would show that forecasting past offsets cannot replace inference from the current episode.

TITLE: Shift-invariant state encoders learned by trajectory-level contrast
PROPOSAL: We pretrain an encoder on the offline dataset with a contrastive objective in which two views of the same trajectory segment differ only by a per-dimension additive constant sampled anew for each view, while segments from different trajectories or with different actions are negatives. The encoder is thus pushed to represent the segment through quantities that an episode-constant shift leaves unchanged, such as velocities, contact timing and action-conditioned changes, and we then train an IQL policy on the frozen encoder output of a window of the last ten observations. Evaluation uses D4RL locomotion, AntMaze and Adroit datasets with test-time offsets from recorded sensor-drift and recalibration series applied per episode, and we measure return along the stream as well as a linear probe of how much offset information survives in the embedding.
CONTROLS: IQL on raw observations, IQL on the same window with an encoder trained without the shift augmentation, an encoder trained with Gaussian-noise views instead of constant shifts, and the policy given offset-free observations as an upper reference.
COST: 350
PREDICTION: The shift-contrastive encoder should keep most of its clean return on locomotion while the noise-view encoder should not, and the probe should recover almost no offset. On AntMaze the loss of absolute position may cost part of the return, which would mark the limit of pure invariance.

TITLE: Shift-invariant state encoders learned by trajectory-level contrast
PROPOSAL: We pretrain an encoder on the offline dataset with a contrastive objective in which two views of the same trajectory segment differ only by a per-dimension additive constant sampled anew for each view, while segments from different trajectories or with different actions are negatives. TITLE: Identifiability conditions for an episode-constant observation offset
PROPOSAL: We give a formal account of identifiability for the test-time setting with additive offsets. With a known deterministic transition function, the offset is identified after k steps exactly when the stacked Jacobians of the corrected transition residuals with respect to the offset have full column rank, and we derive the minimal k for linear systems and for systems whose dynamics are locally affine. Numerically we verify the rank condition on learned dynamics models of D4RL Hopper, Walker2d and AntMaze datasets, counting the number of steps until the condition holds along test episodes with offsets taken from recorded series.

COST: 40

TITLE: Set-membership planning under offsets consistent with the episode so far
PROPOSAL: We combine a learned dynamics ensemble with model-predictive planning in which the unknown offset is not estimated to a point but kept as a set: after each step, the set of offsets consistent with every transition seen so far is tightened using the ensemble's disagreement as the error bound on each residual, giving a box per dimension. The planner samples action sequences, evaluates each on the corners and the centre of the current box with a frozen TD3+BC value function as terminal reward, and executes the first action of the sequence with the best worst-case return. We run the method on D4RL HalfCheetah, Hopper and AntMaze-umaze datasets and on Adroit door, with test offsets from recorded series of recalibration jumps and slow drift, reporting return along an ordered stream and the box width over steps.
CONTROLS: The same planner with the box replaced by its centre point, the planner on uncorrected observations, the planner with the true offset, and the planner with the ensemble disagreement replaced by a fixed error bound.
COST: 520
PREDICTION: Worst-case planning should pay off early in the episode and converge to the centre-point planner as the box shrinks. If the fixed-bound variant performs equally, the ensemble disagreement is not what makes the set tight enough to matter.

Problem statement:
Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning enables large language models to solve complex problems by generating explicit intermediate steps before producing a final answer. Motivated by this success, recent work has sought to extend CoT to the multi-modal domain, aiming to endow multi-modal large language models (MLLMs) with analogous step-by-step reasoning abilities for challenging vision–language tasks.

Despite this progress, modeling coherent multi-modal reasoning remains difficult. TITLE: Encoding only what changed between successive visual states
PROPOSAL: We train Show-o to represent each intermediate visual state not as a full image but as the set of discrete image tokens that differ from the previous state, with their positions, so that a move in a maze or a swap in a jigsaw costs a handful of tokens while a complete redraw remains possible. We report accuracy on held-out tasks, the average number of visual tokens per step, and the fidelity of the reconstructed states to the rendered ones.
CONTROLS: Full-image interleaving at equal training data, text-only chains, direct answers, a fixed random subset of token positions of the same size as the detector's choice, and the model with the state cache disabled so that changes must be inferred from context alone.

PREDICTION: Change encoding should cut visual tokens per step by an order of magnitude on navigation and jigsaw with no loss of accuracy, and lose some fidelity on landscape generation where most of the image changes. If the random-subset variant matches it, position selection is not what matters.

TITLE: A simulator-grounded corpus of interleaved visual reasoning chains
PROPOSAL: We generate a training corpus in which each example pairs a problem with a chain alternating textual steps and rendered visual states produced by a simulator: grid mazes with the agent's path drawn step by step, jigsaw puzzles with pieces placed one at a time, topographic contour maps progressively turned into landscape layouts, and geometry constructions with auxiliary lines added. CONTROLS: The same models fine-tuned on text-only versions of the chains in which each visual state is replaced by a textual description of equal content, on final-answer supervision only, on chains with the visual states shuffled across steps, and training on half the corpus.
COST: 1000
PREDICTION: Interleaved supervision should beat text-described chains on navigation and jigsaw and by less on geometry. If shuffled visual states train as well, the models are ignoring the images and the corpus is working as extra text.

TITLE: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards on interleaved chains
PROPOSAL: We fine-tune Bagel with group-relative policy optimisation on maze navigation, jigsaw solving and geometry tasks where a simulator checks the final answer, and we extend the reward with a term that checks each intermediate visual state against the simulator's own state after the described step. Despite this progress, modeling coherent multi-modal reasoning remains difficult. Efforts to strengthen the text-based reasoning of MLLMs, for example through reinforcement learning, have performed poorly on visually grounded tasks such as geometry or navigation. TITLE: Summarising past visual states into a few learned cache tokens
PROPOSAL: Train Bagel so that, after each visual reasoning step, the thousands of tokens of that visual state are replaced in the key-value cache by thirty-two learned summary tokens produced by a cross-attention module reading the state, while the text tokens stay untouched. PREDICTION: Learned summaries should match full retention on tasks that refer back to earlier states, such as editing, and dropping earlier states should hurt there but not on navigation. If mean pooling is as good, the cross-attention module is not needed.

Efforts to strengthen the text-based reasoning of MLLMs, for example through reinforcement learning, have performed poorly on visually grounded tasks such as geometry or navigation. Humans, by contrast, solve such problems readily by integrating visual state transitions into their reasoning, for instance by updating a map while navigating. This gap calls for models that explicitly represent how the visual state changes during reasoning, rather than approximating these transitions through text. Existing attempts fall short in different ways. Programmatic visual operations such as cropping, drawing or plotting approximate local changes but fail to capture the global structural transformations required by tasks such as navigation, rearrangement or jigsaw solving. Other approaches couple an MLLM with a separate image or video generator, or refine outputs with external reward models, in order to model larger visual changes; however, such loosely integrated designs often lead to fragmented reasoning flows and incoherent visual transitions.

This motivates reasoning in which textual logic and visual state transitions are produced as one coherent process, within a single model that can both understand and generate images and can be trained end to end. Realizing such unified multi-modal reasoning, however, raises two fundamental difficulties. The first is computational burden. Every multi-modal reasoning step must produce and consume both textual and visual intermediates: a text-only reasoning step typically takes a few hundred tokens, whereas generating an image and encoding it again for understanding adds thousands of visual tokens per step, inflating sequence lengths by orders of magnitude relative to text-only reasoning. Because each step of standard autoregressive generation attends to the entire preceding history, the cost grows quadratically with the length of the chain, making both training and inference prohibitively expensive. The second is training instability. Such long sequences complicate long-range dependency modeling and optimization, and interleaved image–text generation further destabilizes training because of mismatched cross-modal dynamics, which can hinder convergence and limit generalization, especially on tasks that demand long, compositional reasoning chains.

This leads to the central question: how can a single model carry out chain-of-thought reasoning that tightly interleaves textual logic with explicit visual state transitions, while keeping the cost of long multi-modal reasoning chains tractable and its training stable? Answering it requires reasoning that is affordable to train and run and that genuinely improves performance on reasoning-intensive tasks, both when understanding visual content and when generating images from prompts that require reasoning.

Problem statement:
The rapid advancement of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) has enabled highly capable AI assistants that can understand and generate complex information across modalities. This capability is valuable for current AI systems and crucial for future human–AI collaboration. However, to collaborate effectively, existing systems often require users to design intricate prompts to convey their intentions and to personalize the assistant's responses. This raises an essential question: can existing MLLMs enable a more proactive AI user experience, in which the assistant seamlessly infers the user's underlying intention and delivers personalized content without relying heavily on complex prompting?

Egocentric (first-person) video is a promising avenue toward this goal. Its viewpoint aligns human visual perception, attention, action and the surrounding scene context within the same egocentric coordinate system, and thereby offers valuable insight into an individual's experiences, actions and intentions. Despite this potential for more personalized and proactive assistance, existing MLLMs have been predominantly developed and evaluated on exocentric video benchmarks. Recent egocentric video question answering benchmarks target episodic memory, long-form video reasoning, scene layout analysis and scene-text understanding, but they overlook a crucial egocentric cue: gaze, which provides direct insight into user attention and intent. For an egocentric AI assistant, most user questions are likely to be inherently conditioned on what the user is looking at, and a model without access to gaze signals may fail on questions about the user's own fixation and focus.

The connection between gaze and action from the first-person viewpoint has been studied before, for instance through gaze-indexed visual features for action recognition, gaze events toward objects for action forecasting, joint modeling of gaze and actions, and dedicated architectures for gaze estimation and anticipation. Yet how gaze cues could help MLLMs answer questions about a user's intentions and actions from an egocentric perspective has not been explored; a recent system (GazeGPT) suggested that gaze data can help design better MLLM user interfaces, but a standardized benchmark and evaluation of this capability are still missing. The problem is also challenging on the model side: MLLMs commonly construct their visual tokens from global image frames, which provide broad scene context but carry no explicit signal of what the camera wearer is attending to, and gaze-related signals are rarely seen during MLLM training, so models may have limited capacity to interpret gaze cues even when such cues are provided.

This leaves several open questions. How can one rigorously assess whether MLLMs understand a camera wearer's intentions in everyday egocentric videos, and whether they can exploit egocentric gaze signals to do so? How well do current MLLMs interpret user intent from egocentric video without gaze information? How should gaze information be presented to an MLLM so that it actually improves the model's understanding of the user's focus and intention? Given that gaze is largely absent from MLLM training data, can the models' limited ability to interpret gaze cues be overcome? And, since accurate eye tracking is not always available, how much does any benefit depend on the accuracy of the gaze signal supplied?

TITLE: Dwell-Time Triggers for Proactive Assistant Suggestions
PROPOSAL: Simulate a proactive assistant on 500 egocentric clips with eye tracking, where a suggestion appears whenever the fixation rests on one object longer than a threshold. Generate each suggestion with an open multimodal model given the frames and the fixated object, then have raters score relevance and timeliness on a five-point scale. Problem statement:
The rapid advancement of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) has enabled highly capable AI assistants that can understand and generate complex information across modalities. This capability is valuable for current AI systems and crucial for future human–AI collaboration. However, to collaborate effectively, existing systems often require users to design intricate prompts to convey their intentions and to personalize the assistant's responses. This raises an essential question: can existing MLLMs enable a more proactive AI user experience, in which the assistant seamlessly infers the user's underlying intention and delivers personalized content without relying heavily on complex prompting?

Egocentric (first-person) video is a promising avenue toward this goal. Its viewpoint aligns human visual perception, attention, action and the surrounding scene context within the same egocentric coordinate system, and thereby offers valuable insight into an individual's experiences, actions and intentions. Despite this potential for more personalized and proactive assistance, existing MLLMs have been predominantly developed and evaluated on exocentric video benchmarks. Recent egocentric video question answering benchmarks target episodic memory, long-form video reasoning, scene layout analysis and scene-text understanding, but they overlook a crucial egocentric cue: gaze, which provides direct insight into user attention and intent. For an egocentric AI assistant, most user questions are likely to be inherently conditioned on what the user is looking at, and a model without access to gaze signals may fail on questions about the user's own fixation and focus.

The connection between gaze and action from the first-person viewpoint has been studied before, for instance through gaze-indexed visual features for action recognition, gaze events toward objects for action forecasting, joint modeling of gaze and actions, and dedicated architectures for gaze estimation and anticipation. Problem statement:
Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have made remarkable progress in multimodal understanding and reasoning by combining Large Language Models (LLMs) with powerful pre-trained visual encoders whose features are projected into the language model's semantic space. This design, however, is asymmetric: such models treat images only as inputs and cannot generate them, which limits the synergy between perception and synthesis. To enable that synergy, recent efforts have moved toward Unified Multimodal Models (UMMs), which aim to support both understanding and generation within a single framework.

Many advanced UMMs rely on increasingly complex system designs to boost performance: adding semantic image encoders, hybridizing autoregressive and diffusion paradigms, or introducing task-specific branches and experts, such as Mixture-of-Transformers designs that route understanding and generation through distinct transformer branches, or forks that add task-specific deep heads. While effective on benchmarks, this added complexity hinders scalability and complicates training; it also limits the degree of parameter sharing and reduces the potential for mutual benefits across tasks and modalities, which are the very goals that unified models were meant to achieve.

Autoregressive (AR) UMMs offer a simple yet powerful alternative. By treating visual inputs as a "foreign language" through vector quantization, they turn text and images into one consistent sequence of discrete tokens trained with next-token prediction, naturally extending the language-centric paradigm of LLMs. Yet the distinct statistical properties of text and images often lead to modality conflicts that degrade performance when a single transformer is shared across both modalities, and why and where these conflicts arise inside the network remains poorly understood. In multi-task learning, this kind of interference has been studied as gradient conflict: different optimization objectives induce gradients pointing in divergent directions, making joint optimization unstable and inefficient. This lens has not been systematically applied to the interplay between modalities inside unified models, and applying it is not straightforward, since transformer layers are known to play distinct roles at different depths, with representations becoming increasingly abstract and semantic in intermediate layers.

This raises several questions. How can the disagreement between text and vision gradients in a modality-shared AR transformer be quantified in a principled, layer-wise way? Do inter-modal conflicts vary along the depth of the network, and to what extent can they be explained by fundamental differences between the statistics of discretized image-token sequences and those of natural language? Finally, can an AR UMM be designed to respect modality-specific differences, reducing these conflicts and improving training efficiency and performance, while preserving the architectural simplicity, broad parameter sharing and scalability of a pure autoregressive model, rather than resorting to auxiliary encoders, diffusion hybrids or task-specific branches?

TITLE: Per-Layer Gradient Cosine Between Text and Image Losses
PROPOSAL: Take a publicly released autoregressive model that reads and writes both text and discrete image tokens, and measure how text-loss gradients and image-loss gradients agree in each transformer layer. Draw 2000 caption-image pairs, split them into separate data slices, compute both gradients for every layer on each slice, and record cosine similarity plus the fraction of parameters whose gradient signs differ. Plot both quantities against depth with intervals across slices.
CONTROLS: Compare the cross-modal cosine with the cosine between two text slices and between two image slices at each layer. Repeat on a second checkpoint of the same model, and on three random orders of the slices.
COST: 150
PREDICTION: Cross-modal cosine should sit below the within-modality values in the middle layers. The finding is undermined if both within-modality values are as low as the cross-modal one.

Problem statement:
Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have made remarkable progress in multimodal understanding and reasoning by combining Large Language Models (LLMs) with powerful pre-trained visual encoders whose features are projected into the language model's semantic space. This design, however, is asymmetric: such models treat images only as inputs and cannot generate them, which limits the synergy between perception and synthesis. To enable that synergy, recent efforts have moved toward Unified Multimodal Models (UMMs), which aim to support both understanding and generation within a single framework.

Many advanced UMMs rely on increasingly complex system designs to boost performance: adding semantic image encoders, hybridizing autoregressive and diffusion paradigms, or introducing task-specific branches and experts, such as Mixture-of-Transformers designs that route understanding and generation through distinct transformer branches, or forks that add task-specific deep heads. While effective on benchmarks, this added complexity hinders scalability and complicates training; it also limits the degree of parameter sharing and reduces the potential for mutual benefits across tasks and modalities, which are the very goals that unified models were meant to achieve.

Autoregressive (AR) UMMs offer a simple yet powerful alternative. By treating visual inputs as a "foreign language" through vector quantization, they turn text and images into one consistent sequence of discrete tokens trained with next-token prediction, naturally extending the language-centric paradigm of LLMs. Yet the distinct statistical properties of text and images often lead to modality conflicts that degrade performance when a single transformer is shared across both modalities, and why and where these conflicts arise inside the network remains poorly understood. In multi-task learning, this kind of interference has been studied as gradient conflict: different optimization objectives induce gradients pointing in divergent directions, making joint optimization unstable and inefficient. This lens has not been systematically applied to the interplay between modalities inside unified models, and applying it is not straightforward, since transformer layers are known to play distinct roles at different depths, with representations becoming increasingly abstract and semantic in intermediate layers.

This raises several questions. How can the disagreement between text and vision gradients in a modality-shared AR transformer be quantified in a principled, layer-wise way? Do inter-modal conflicts vary along the depth of the network, and to what extent can they be explained by fundamental differences between the statistics of discretized image-token sequences and those of natural language? Finally, can an AR UMM be designed to respect modality-specific differences, reducing these conflicts and improving training efficiency and performance, while preserving the architectural simplicity, broad parameter sharing and scalability of a pure autoregressive model, rather than resorting to auxiliary encoders, diffusion hybrids or task-specific branches?

Problem statement:
Emotion understanding is essential for social AI agents to generate tailored responses and foster meaningful human-machine interactions. Emotion perception also finds applications in domains such as health and education, where appropriately responding to affective states can improve therapeutic alliance and learning outcomes.

Traditional multimodal emotion recognition methods lack interpretability, as they only perform classification without grounding their outputs in audiovisual cues. Moreover, emotion is a complex and multi-componential construct that extends beyond the basic emotion labels that can be assigned by supervised learning methods. To address these challenges, recent approaches leverage multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to generate detailed emotion descriptions for interpretability and to output emotion-related keywords that cover a broader spectrum of emotional states.

However, audiovisual MLLMs are susceptible to hallucinations, frequently generating inaccurate or fabricated responses. In the context of emotion understanding, they face two critical bottlenecks. First, these models often ground emotion predictions on irrelevant cues (e.g., attire color, ambient noise), which can be called reasoning errors. Second, they tend to hallucinate additional cues in their responses to justify emotions, which can be called perception errors. Such hallucinations are largely driven by text priors in the language model backbone, which bias the model to include cues that commonly co-occur with specific emotions (e.g., associating tears with the sound of crying). The scarcity of high-quality, emotion-specific instruction tuning data further aggravates these issues. Addressing these challenges is essential, as they compromise the reliability of MLLM agents in social interactions and complex emotion reasoning scenarios.

Measuring these failure modes is itself difficult. Existing emotion reasoning benchmarks lack the diverse and complex samples needed to fully evaluate them; current audiovisual hallucination benchmarks predominantly focus on object-level hallucinations in audio or video rather than on emotion-specific reasoning; and many existing emotion-oriented MLLMs rely on two-stage evaluation pipelines involving an external, often proprietary, LLM, making replication and benchmarking difficult.

This leaves two open questions. How can audiovisual MLLMs be evaluated in a transparent, reproducible and scalable way for emotion reasoning, in particular for whether they tie emotions to the audiovisual cues that actually explain them rather than to irrelevant cues, and whether they invent cues that are absent from the input? And how can such models be made to ground their emotion predictions and explanations in the audio and visual evidence actually present, rather than in spurious cue-emotion associations and in the text priors of their language backbone?

TITLE: Contrastive decoding against modality-dropped inputs
PROPOSAL: Reduce text-prior hallucination at inference time by contrasting the next-token distribution of the full audiovisual input with the distribution obtained when the clip is replaced by a blank frame and silence. Tokens that stay likely without the clip are penalised, so the explanation keeps only cues that the audio or the frames actually support. Apply the decoding rule to an open audiovisual language model on the DFEW and MAFW test clips, tune the penalty strength on a small validation split, and score the outputs with a keyword lexicon of annotated cues and with emotion keyword accuracy. No training is needed, so the method can be tried on any model whose logits are accessible.
CONTROLS: The comparison runs are greedy decoding, nucleus sampling, and the same contrastive rule with only the audio track dropped or only the frames dropped, all on the same clips and seeds. A shuffled-clip run, where the contrast input comes from a different clip, shows whether the gain comes from removing text priors or from plain regularisation of the distribution.
COST: 190
PREDICTION: Invented cues should fall while emotion keyword accuracy stays within a point of greedy decoding. The idea fails if the shuffled-clip contrast removes as many invented cues as the blank contrast, or if accuracy drops sharply.

Problem statement:
Emotion understanding is essential for social AI agents to generate tailored responses and foster meaningful human-machine interactions. Emotion perception also finds applications in domains such as health and education, where appropriately responding to affective states can improve therapeutic alliance and learning outcomes.

Traditional multimodal emotion recognition methods lack interpretability, as they only perform classification without grounding their outputs in audiovisual cues. Moreover, emotion is a complex and multi-componential construct that extends beyond the basic emotion labels that can be assigned by supervised learning methods. To address these challenges, recent approaches leverage multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to generate detailed emotion descriptions for interpretability and to output emotion-related keywords that cover a broader spectrum of emotional states.

However, audiovisual MLLMs are susceptible to hallucinations, frequently generating inaccurate or fabricated responses. In the context of emotion understanding, they face two critical bottlenecks. First, these models often ground emotion predictions on irrelevant cues (e.g., attire color, ambient noise), which can be called reasoning errors. Second, they tend to hallucinate additional cues in their responses to justify emotions, which can be called perception errors. Such hallucinations are largely driven by text priors in the language model backbone, which bias the model to include cues that commonly co-occur with specific emotions (e.g., associating tears with the sound of crying). The scarcity of high-quality, emotion-specific instruction tuning data further aggravates these issues. Addressing these challenges is essential, as they compromise the reliability of MLLM agents in social interactions and complex emotion reasoning scenarios.

Measuring these failure modes is itself difficult. Existing emotion reasoning benchmarks lack the diverse and complex samples needed to fully evaluate them; current audiovisual hallucination benchmarks predominantly focus on object-level hallucinations in audio or video rather than on emotion-specific reasoning; and many existing emotion-oriented MLLMs rely on two-stage evaluation pipelines involving an external, often proprietary, LLM, making replication and benchmarking difficult.

This leaves two open questions. How can audiovisual MLLMs be evaluated in a transparent, reproducible and scalable way for emotion reasoning, in particular for whether they tie emotions to the audiovisual cues that actually explain them rather than to irrelevant cues, and whether they invent cues that are absent from the input? And how can such models be made to ground their emotion predictions and explanations in the audio and visual evidence actually present, rather than in spurious cue-emotion associations and in the text priors of their language backbone?

TITLE: Locating attention heads that import text priors in emotion explanations
PROPOSAL: Analyse an open seven-billion-parameter audiovisual model on DFEW clips for the heads whose attention to audio and frame tokens is weak while they write cue words. For each generated cue phrase, record the share of attention mass on the clip tokens per head, then select the heads with the lowest share and intervene by scaling their outputs down or boosting the heads with the highest clip share. Measure whether invented cues decrease and whether irrelevant but present cues, such as clothing colour or room noise, are cited less often as the reason for an emotion. Cue presence is checked against annotator lists, so no external judge is used.
CONTROLS: Compare the targeted intervention with scaling the same number of randomly chosen heads, and with no intervention. Repeat the head selection on two disjoint halves of the clips to test stability, and track keyword accuracy to see whether general quality is damaged.
COST: 130
PREDICTION: Boosting clip-attending heads should reduce invented cues more than scaling random heads. The idea fails if head selection does not transfer across the two halves, or if keyword accuracy falls as much as invented cues do.

TITLE: Training a cue verifier to filter emotion explanations
PROPOSAL: Train a lightweight verifier that reads a clip embedding and one cue statement and predicts whether the cue is present. Positive statements come from annotator cue lists on MAFW and DFEW, negatives from absent cues that commonly co-occur with the labelled emotion, such as tears with crying sounds. Use the verifier for rejection sampling: draw sixteen explanations per clip from an audiovisual language model, keep those whose cues all pass, and fine-tune on the kept ones. Evaluate unsupported-cue rate and emotion keyword accuracy on held-out clips, and report the verifier's own precision on absent but typical cues.
CONTROLS: Compare against fine-tuning on randomly kept explanations, against a verifier that sees only the text statement, and against the untuned model. Fix the sampling budget and the update count across runs, and use three seeds.
COST: 350
PREDICTION: A verifier that sees the clip should beat a text-only verifier on absent but typical cues by a clear gap in precision. The approach fails if the text-only verifier performs equally well, because then the filter would only copy language priors.

TITLE: Conflict stimuli for testing which cue drives an emotion explanation
PROPOSAL: We construct conflict clips by pairing emotional speech from CREMA-D with face videos of a different emotion, and by adding irrelevant cues such as a bright jacket or street noise. We ask open audiovisual language models to name the emotion and justify it. Because we know which modality carries the labelled emotion in each clip, we can score automatically whether the justification cites the cue that actually explains the label, an irrelevant cue, or a cue absent from the input. We parse justifications with a fixed lexicon, so the evaluation needs no external language model and anyone can replay it. We then fine-tune one model on conflict clips with correct justifications and test it on unseen speakers.
CONTROLS: We compare the models against a text-only prompt and against clips where both modalities agree. We repeat every measurement with five seeds and check the lexicon parser against manual labels on two hundred justifications.
COST: 60
PREDICTION: We expect most justifications to cite the dominant modality of the model rather than the modality that carries the label. We would see the idea fail if the parser disagrees with manual labels or if agreeing clips show the same error rate as conflict clips.

Problem statement:

Emotion perception also finds applications in domains such as health and education, where appropriately responding to affective states can improve therapeutic alliance and learning outcomes.

TITLE: Distractor augmentation to teach invariance to irrelevant cues
PROPOSAL: Teach a model to ignore irrelevant cues by editing training clips. Recolour clothing in frames, mix ambient street or cafe noise into the audio, and swap backgrounds, while leaving facial expression and voice prosody untouched.
